# library and Yul Parsing Decisions

This was first written down because the library contract kind, the legacy AST field, and Yul top-level identifiers all came up in compatibility investigations, and discussions would quickly conflate the three kinds of object into one issue. This records the distinctions drawn at the time and the provisional choices, to avoid later putting inputs from different layers on the same fix path just because "the names don't match."

The working judgment at the time was: declaration parsing should preserve the kind of a contract declaration; type parsing should not guess a declaration's kind from the legacy field. `slither/solc_parsing/solidity_types/type_parsing.py` can help locate code around type conversion, but it should not be responsible for building out a contract model from a AST-shaped input. This part of the code touches the links between types and declaration objects, but that does not mean it can be the decision point for every input format.

Another choice was to treat Yul top-level identifiers separately. Even when one looks like a Solidity name, it cannot simply be sent down the contract-declaration handling path on that basis. Keep it within identifier resolution, and wait for a reproducible input before deciding whether any lookup logic needs to be shared. Identical names establish only that the text is the same, not that both sides have the same scope, declaration information, or subsequent state.

An easier approach was proposed during review: first normalize legacy and compact nodes, then fill in library from the normalized name field. This approach was not adopted. Field normalization can be a convenience at the reader layer, but it must not silently change declaration kinds; otherwise, it would be impossible to tell whether the flag seen downstream came from the original AST or was inferred.

At this point, the decision is to keep two boundaries:

- Contract-kind compatibility is the responsibility of the declaration model, not type-string conversion.
- Investigate Yul top-level identifier issues along the lookup path first; do not treat these identifiers as aliases for legacy Solidity AST.

There is not yet enough information to decide whether to fall back, report an error, or skip when a legacy node is missing an expected field. There is also no evidence showing whether the Yul issue occurs before or after lookup. This gap is left open here to avoid mixing nodes from different sources just to let a single parse continue.

# Parsing Decisions for library and Yul

This was first documented because the library contract kind, legacy AST fields, and Yul top-level identifiers all came up during compatibility investigation, and discussions would quickly conflate the three kinds of objects into a single issue. The earliest notes were only intended to prevent a very common fix: routing nodes in different formats through the same declaration construction path simply because their names looked similar.

At the time, the working judgment was: the kind of a contract declaration should be preserved by declaration parsing; type parsing should not guess a declaration's kind based on legacy fields. `slither/solc_parsing/solidity_types/type_parsing.py` can help locate code near type conversion, but it should not be responsible for filling in a AST shape to produce a contract model. This file is a related touchpoint to revisit during investigation, not the place to collapse legacy and compact formats into the same kind of node.

Another choice was to treat Yul top-level identifiers separately. Even when one looks like a Solidity name, that is no reason to put it directly on the contract declaration processing path. Keep it within identifier resolution for now, and wait for a reproducible input before deciding whether any lookup logic needs to be shared. The fact that name text can be looked up does not mean the lookup side has the context required for contract declarations.

## Initial Choices

During review, a simpler approach was proposed: first normalize legacy and compact nodes, then infer library from the normalized name field. This approach was not adopted. Field normalization can be a convenience in the reading layer, but it must not silently change the declaration kind; otherwise it becomes impossible to tell whether a flag seen later came from the original AST or was inferred after the fact.

The two boundaries set out in the earliest notes still hold: compatibility for contract kinds is the responsibility of the declaration model, not type-string conversion; anomalies involving Yul top-level identifiers should first be investigated along the lookup path, without treating those identifiers as aliases for legacy Solidity AST. Here, "responsibility" does not mean that every part is completely isolated, but that later type processing must not silently take over the decision about the kind of the input object.

## Connections Observed During Review

After reviewing the paths, the original statement needed to be narrowed. The type parsing file contains dependencies such as `logging`, `re`, as well as `List`, `TYPE_CHECKING`, `Union`, `Dict`, and `ValuesView`; it also imports `CustomErrorContract`. This shows that this code has to deal with type conversion branches, collection shapes, and objects from the declaration side. It does not show that type parsing owns all declaration compatibility rules.

Someone had previously speculated on this basis that simply adding a legacy-field branch near type parsing would solve both the library and Yul issues. This speculation was not accepted after review. Importing a declaration object and deciding which kind of AST to build that declaration object from are two different things. The former is a downstream usage relationship, while the latter involves reading the raw node, confirming what fields mean, and making judgments before constructing the common model.

Field differences in legacy AST are also not limited to a single name field. The locations of a node's children, the declaration name, and the kind information are not guaranteed to be at the same level. If they are merged into a generic dictionary too early, missing fields and changes in field semantics will both be recorded as the same "null value", and subsequent code will only see an object whose provenance has already been lost.

The additional decision this time is therefore not "never normalize", but to restrict where normalization takes place: when reading a particular kind of AST, the node information explicitly provided by that format may be extracted; before entering the common declaration model, it must still be possible to tell which kind of AST that information came from; names that happen to be visible in the legacy format must not be used to infer the contract kind in the compact format; type conversion accepts only types or declaration objects that have already been determined, and does not take on the task of filling in raw nodes.

The second point was added only after the review. The old notes focused only on whether the output could continue downstream, overlooking a more practical issue: once library and ordinary contracts are merged at the input stage, downstream callers receive models that look the same, but do not know whether one of the flags is reliable. Errors in the compatibility layer will surface farther downstream, making investigation harder instead.

## An Attempt That Was Not Pursued

Reusing Solidity's declaration-name lookup order for Yul top-level identifiers was considered. The reasoning was straightforward: both appear as a name to be resolved, and reusing the path seemed to avoid writing an extra branch. This idea did not become a decision.

The problem is that this does not automatically give Yul top-level identifiers the context of Solidity contract declarations. Sending one through the same name path may produce a seemingly reasonable object, or may leave an incomplete resolution result in the subsequent state. The existing records point only to an "abnormal state after processing", without confirming any particular field, scope, or type conversion as the cause.

Therefore, the current choice is to suspend sharing: the Yul side may reuse only those lookup steps already proven relevant to top-level identifiers; when contract kinds, inheritance relationships, or declaration flags are involved, it must return to its own context. This suspension is not a rejection of Yul, but is intended to prevent a convenient bit of reuse from locking two different naming systems together.

## Retained Earlier Passage

The following passage states the earliest working approach and is retained to explain why the integration approach was changed later:

> When names in legacy AST are stable enough, nodes can first be classified by name, then the library-specific distinctions can be added to the common model; Yul names can follow the same path, with later parsing providing fault tolerance when information is missing.

This passage no longer applies. The problem is not the term "fault tolerance" itself, but that it combines missing input, format differences, and object kinds into a single recovery action. Continuing downstream when fields are missing is not necessarily recovery; it may also mean recording a judgment of unknown provenance as an established fact.

The replacement decision is to preserve differences between input formats until the kind has been determined. For nodes whose kind cannot be determined, the issue should remain at the parsing boundary, rather than allowing a name to disguise them as a different kind of declaration.

## Unanswered Questions

The Yul top-level identifier example still lacks a fixed input and corresponding output. What needs to be added is material showing whether the anomaly occurs before, during, or after lookup, not another summary containing only names.

The specific strategy for legacy AST when fields are incomplete is also undecided. Whether the reading layer can retain an incomplete node for upstream reporting, or must stop during reading, still needs to be decided in conjunction with the existing test entry points. For now, this gap will not be filled with default behavior.

# library and Yul parsing decision

This record begins with a set of issues that can easily obscure one another: library is a declaration kind, the fields of the legacy AST describe the input shape, and top-level Yul identifiers belong to a different name-resolution context. They were all once described as "the names didn't match," but that wording cannot explain why later models continued running with the wrong kind, nor why the state after a given processing step was abnormal.

The earliest adjacent point found during the investigation was `slither/solc_parsing/solidity_types/type_parsing.py`. The file's `logging`, `re`, `List`, `TYPE_CHECKING`, `Union`, `Dict`, and `ValuesView` indicate that this location handles both conversion branches and the requirements for type checking and collection shape; the import of `CustomErrorContract` makes it very easy to mistake this for the general entry point for declaration compatibility. Later, responsibilities were not expanded based on that impression: type resolution can connect to declaration objects, but what kind of AST a declaration object was built from should be determined closer to the original node.

This page does not attempt to combine library, legacy nodes, and Yul into a single fault label. The three are adjacent, but their causes may differ: for library, what must be preserved is the contract kind; for legacy AST, what needs to be explained is what node shape the field is in; for a top-level Yul identifier, what needs to be confirmed is whether name lookup borrowed a declaration context that does not belong to it. Describing all of them as "compatibility branches" would make later readers mistakenly think they only need to add one condition in one file.

## 2023-05: Earliest Recorded Decision

The initial decision was narrow: do not infer the contract kind from legacy fields at the type-resolution stage. Legacy nodes and compact nodes can share some downstream objects after being read, but they cannot be collapsed into the same data before their kind is known. The reason is not that the field names themselves are particularly unusual; it is that once library and ordinary contracts are merged at the entry point, even if a usable object is obtained later, it is impossible to tell whether differences in that object came from the source input.

At the same time, top-level Yul identifiers were treated separately. On the surface, it is also a name to look up, but there was no evidence that it carries the scope and kind information of a Solidity contract declaration. The initial handling choice was not to force it through the declaration-construction path; instead, retain it as an identifier-resolution issue and wait for examples that could show when the state becomes abnormal.
At the time, a shortcut was also discussed: first put legacy nodes and compact nodes into the same common structure, then infer library from the normalized name. This approach was not adopted as the decision. Field normalization can reduce read branches, but it must not silently change the declaration kind; once that happens, there is no way to distinguish whether the flag seen later came from the original AST or from a subsequent inference.

Two boundaries were retained from the outset. Contract-kind compatibility is handled by the declaration model, not by type-string conversion. An anomaly in a Yul top-level identifier should first be investigated along the lookup path, rather than treated as an alias of legacy Solidity AST. These two points do not mean that code cannot be shared; they limit where sharing may occur: local steps that depend only on name text can be reconsidered, but steps that depend on declaration kind must not be reused directly just because the names match.

At the time, there was not enough evidence to decide whether legacy nodes missing expected fields should fall back, raise an error, or be skipped. Nor was there evidence showing whether the Yul anomaly occurred before, during, or after lookup. The early record deliberately stopped here, so that "try to continue parsing as much as possible" would not become a default rule without evidence from the input.

## Early Review Margin Note

The first review did not overturn the above separation, but it surfaced an implicit issue: if "compatibility" is understood as "normalize all formats as quickly as possible", the common model receives an object that looks uniform, while callers cannot see what type of input the object originally came from. The fact that the model can continue to be passed along does not mean that its kind determination is trustworthy.

Accordingly, the post-review wording was changed to describe two layers. The reading layer is responsible for identifying what a given format actually provides; the common model accepts only conclusions that already establish the source of the kind. Type-string conversion handles only type relationships that already exist; it is not responsible for repairing raw nodes into contract declarations. This addendum may look like merely a division of responsibilities, but it actually determines where to investigate: if the input format has not yet been confirmed, go back to the reading layer; if the kind has been determined but the downstream object does not behave correctly, look at the declaration model; do not hand both types of issue to type conversion.

The suggestion to fill all missing parts with null also came up in the review. The reason given at the time was to reduce the number of format branches in later logic. It was not adopted, because null only indicates that a given position has no value; it cannot distinguish between two different situations: one is that this AST format does not provide that information here at all, and the other is that the input should have contained the information but is incomplete. For contract kinds, these two situations cannot be collapsed into the same null value.

One rhetorical question left at the time was useful: if a model already carries a library flag but has not retained the determination of which kind of input the flag came from, who can explain that flag later? This is not a requirement for every object to carry a complete history; it is a requirement that, before the kind is decided, no other field can stand in for it. Names, sub-item structure, and kind information may appear next to each other, but that does not make them the same evidence.

## 2023-10: Path Review

After reviewing `type_parsing.py`, the earlier claim that "the compatibility entry point is probably somewhere around type parsing" needs to be narrowed. This file shows `logging`,`re`,`List`,`TYPE_CHECKING`,`Union`,`Dict`,`ValuesView`, and also imports `CustomErrorContract`. These dependencies indicate that it needs to handle connections between various types and declaration objects, not that it determines the origin or kind of every declaration object.

There was once a working assumption: since type parsing touches declaration-side objects, add a branch for legacy fields here and handle library and Yul at the same time. This assumption was abandoned after review. Importing a declaration object is one thing, and deciding how a declaration object is constructed from AST is another. The former indicates that downstream code consumes the object, while the latter requires reading the raw nodes, confirming field semantics, and determining the kind before entering the shared model.

Reviewing the paths also made the issue with legacy AST more concrete. It is not just a difference in "whether a name is present": the locations of node children, declaration names and kind information are not guaranteed to be at the same level. If they are first merged into a generic dictionary, missing fields, changes in field location and changes in field meaning all become the same kind of gap that subsequent code cannot distinguish. Although this can reduce branching, it erases differences between input formats precisely where they most need to be preserved.

So the decision retained in this round is not "never normalize", but to constrain when normalization happens. When reading a particular kind of AST, the node information explicitly provided by that format can be extracted; before entering the shared declaration model, it must still be possible to identify which kind of AST the information came from; a name that happens to be visible in the old format must not be used to infer the contract kind in the compact format; type conversion accepts only types or declaration objects that have already been determined, and does not take on the task of filling in raw nodes.

The second point here was added later. The old notes only considered whether the output could continue downstream, overlooking a more practical scenario: once library contracts and ordinary contracts are merged at the input stage, downstream callers receive the same outward model representation, but do not know whether one of its flags is reliable. Errors in the compatibility layer only surface further downstream, and troubleshooting shifts from an input issue to a seemingly unrelated downstream issue.

## An Inconclusive Yul Attempt

One idea considered was to have Yul top-level identifiers reuse the lookup order for Solidity declaration names. The reasoning was straightforward: both appear as a name to be resolved, and reusing the path seemed to avoid the need for an extra branch. This idea did not become a decision.

The issue is that Yul top-level identifiers do not automatically acquire the context of Solidity contract declarations as a result. Routing one through the same name-resolution path may produce a seemingly plausible object, or it may leave an incomplete resolution result in a later state. The existing exception description only points to "an abnormal state after processing" and does not confirm the cause as any particular field, scope, or type conversion.

At the time, the investigation was narrowed back down to three questions: Had the identifier in the input already been handled as a Solidity declaration; did the lookup process require declaration context; what exactly was missing from the state after processing. The first two questions could be checked along the resolution path, but the third was never completed. Without the third item, the anomaly cannot be definitively attributed to the reading layer, declaration model, or type resolution.

Pausing sharing does not mean refusing reuse. The Yul side only allows reuse of lookup steps already proven to be related to top-level identifiers; when contract kind, inheritance relationships, or declaration flags are involved, it must return to its own context. This leaves some duplicate checks, but the duplication is explicit; incorrectly borrowing context from another naming system causes errors to surface later.

## Previously adopted permissive approach

The earliest working position is retained below, rather than being rewritten into wording that now seems more orderly:

> When the name of the old AST is stable enough, it can first be classified by name, and then the library differences can be filled in on the common model; Yul names can also follow this route, with subsequent parsing tolerating missing information.

This no longer applies. The problem is not reusing name lookup, but mistaking successful name lookup for successful object-kind identification. A name may be found while the declaration context remains incomplete; the state after processing may also already be abnormal, with the issue simply not yet exposed at the current call site.

The old approach was retained because it explains why early investigations repeatedly ended up at the type-resolution files. The common declaration flow appeared to continue downward from there, so it seemed that a compatibility branch should be added at that location. The decision after reviewing the path was not to expand its responsibilities there. `type_parsing.py` is an adjacent point that needs to be checked again, not a location that can make decisions for all AST formats.

The "continue as far as possible" behavior in the old approach was not removed entirely; it was only moved away from kind determination. When a local step does not depend on missing declaration information, parsing may continue; when continuing would create an unsupported contract kind, the issue should be left at the boundary. This distinction avoids conflating stopping parsing with refusing to process.

## Review meeting notes

One comment left during a review was: Do not infer that every source node can reach the same conclusion merely because the common model has a usable library flag. Another comment was more direct: A Yul name anomaly and a key difference in the old-style AST can occur at the same time, but their occurring at the same time does not mean they have the same fix point.

These two comments changed the way subsequent comparisons were made. The comparison was no longer "which branch is shorter," but rather "does this branch preserve the boundary between the input format, object kind, and name context." The former makes the code look uniform; the latter is what allows the common model to explain its own state.

The meeting also kept a counterexample angle in consideration: if a legacy node has a name, but the shape of its child items differs from compact AST, entering the unified flow based on the name alone would cause subsequent traversal to mistakenly assume that the two have the same structure. This counterexample was not written up as a completed test result; it only shows that the name cannot serve as proof of the identity of the entire node.

Another rejected simplification was to have every format retain only three slots—"name, children, kind"—after reading, with the shared layer consuming them by slot. This appears to make the reading layer smaller, but it makes the slots themselves carry the format semantics. If legacy and compact nodes assign different meanings to the same slot, the shared layer cannot determine whether it received an explicit field or a value filled in by the compatibility layer, so this approach was not adopted further.

## Current integration order

The current order is not a general parsing flow; it defines the boundary for this scope: first determine whether the input is a compact AST, a legacy Solidity AST, or a Yul top-level identifier scenario; for the first two categories, read the declaration information explicitly provided by each format, without using fields from the other format to fill gaps; create or update the shared declaration model only after the kind has been determined; type parsing consumes only objects and types that have already been determined and does not reinterpret node kinds; the Yul path reuses only local lookups that do not depend on Solidity declaration context, while the other parts remain independent.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> InputIdentification
    InputIdentification --> CompactAST: contractKind
    InputIdentification --> LegacyAST: NodeKey
    InputIdentification --> YulTopLevelIdentifier
    CompactAST --> DeclarationModel: KindDetermined
    LegacyAST --> DeclarationModel: FormatFieldsRead
    DeclarationModel --> TypeParsing
    YulTopLevelIdentifier --> LocalLookup
    LocalLookup --> YulTopLevelIdentifier: DeclarationContextRequired
    LocalLookup --> [*]: IdentifierOnly
    TypeParsing --> [*]
```

The return to the Yul top-level identifier in the diagram is not an alternative to failure recovery; it only indicates that once local lookup requires the contract kind, inheritance relationships, or declaration hierarchy, it cannot continue borrowing the Solidity declaration path. The old records did not provide a complete failure sample, so the diagram was not drawn as a conclusion that "the exception necessarily occurs at a particular node."

The current order also does not require the reading layer to convert every format into entirely different downstream objects. Sharing can occur once the kind and necessary context are explicit. What is prohibited is using a name, blank slot, or child-item position in one format to fill in the contract kind for another format. This restriction applies both between legacy AST and compact AST, and to the case of mistakenly promoting a Yul name to a Solidity declaration.

## Current requirements

For compact AST, contractKind=library must be retained as the contract kind, and the public library flag is true on that basis. The node children field in non-compact Solidity AST uses the `children` key. The public Contract model maintains consistent observable behavior for `is_library`. Legacy Solidity AST uses the `name` key to identify node names, and package metadata declares the distribution package name through the `name` field.

This requirement rolls back the earlier permissive approach of "classifying by name first". The kind in compact AST comes from the kind information explicitly provided by the format; node names and children in legacy AST are each read according to the legacy format. When the public model receives library information, it should be able to trace it to the contract kind, rather than to a node whose name happens to match.

There are two easily confused `name` here. In legacy Solidity AST, `name` is the node name; in package metadata, `name` is the distribution package name. The two share the same field term, but neither should be used to substantiate any AST compatibility conclusions about the other. Earlier records did not document this ambiguity separately, making it easy in subsequent investigations to describe "seeing a name field" as "finding the contract name". Fields are now interpreted in the context of the object, and identical wording is no longer a reason to merge paths.

Likewise, `children` is not an alias for connecting arbitrary nodes into a unified structure. It is the key that should be used when reading node children in non-compact Solidity AST. The contract kind in compact AST is also not a property inferred indirectly from `children` or `name`. The three terms may appear in the same compatibility documentation, but each still conveys information at a different level.

`is_library` belongs on the public-model side, so it represents an already-determined model state, not a switch that lets the reading layer guess at arbitrary names. If the input is compact AST, the basis for determining its kind is `contractKind=library`; if the input is a legacy Solidity AST, first read the name and child items from the legacy node's fields, and then decide whether there is enough declaration information to enter the public model. This avoids using properties already present in the model as an interpreter for the input format in reverse.

Type utilities remain adjacent to this requirement, but have not taken on any new responsibility for determining kind. Type resolution needs to consume objects and types that have already been determined; even if it encounters `CustomErrorContract`, it cannot infer that it should patch library based on legacy fields. Contract kind belongs to the declaration model, while type relationships belong to type conversion. Their meeting in a single analysis is not a reason for either side to interpret raw nodes on behalf of the other.

## Yul remains separate

The parsing issue for Yul top-level identifiers does not automatically end with the above requirement. At present, all that is established is that it cannot be promoted to a Solidity contract declaration merely because its name looks similar, nor can missing context be filled in using the field conventions of legacy AST.

If subsequent review shows that a Yul lookup step depends only on identifier text, it can be reused locally; if the step requires contract kind, declaration hierarchy, or the child-item structure of AST, it should remain in Yul's own path. This decision does not claim that Yul and Solidity never intersect; it only prevents bringing the assumptions of one naming system into the other before the intersection has been confirmed.

A fixed failing input and its output are still missing. What needs to be added is not a new description of the name, but the point at which the exception occurs: whether the top-level identifier has not yet entered lookup, whether lookup has already returned an object, or whether the state is incomplete after the return. Without this sequence, continuing to add compatibility branches merely moves the location of the problem.

## Adjacent matters not yet separated

The missing-field policy for legacy AST is still undecided. When the input lacks an expected field, whether the reading layer can retain an incomplete node for upstream reporting or should stop immediately depends on whether that field participates in determining the kind. This issue is adjacent to library's current convention, but cannot be covered by the same default policy.

Evidence also needs to be retained for Yul errors so that three locations can be distinguished: the top-level identifier text, the lookup branch entered, and the state after processing. A sample containing only the name and no ordering information cannot support attributing the problem to the reading layer, declaration model, or type resolution.

If a suggestion later appears to "eliminate branches through a generic dictionary," first confirm whether that dictionary can preserve the input format and field semantics. If it cannot, the only thing reduced is the current branch count, while what increases is kind-determination logic that cannot be explained in the public model. This is the reason to withdraw the old approach, not a requirement that all reading code use the same representation.

## Note on an old case

The first old example treated `name` in legacy nodes as evidence "sufficient for classification". This example is retained as a historical reminder, but its conclusion is no longer valid: names can help identify nodes, but cannot establish the contract kind on their own.

The second old example recommended falling back to the name-based path when compact nodes lacked sufficient information. This example is likewise no longer applicable. Kind information explicitly present in the compact format should be preserved; when information is insufficient, gaps must not be filled using the field semantics of another format.

An early note also stated, "If the shared model can run successfully, that means the input is already compatible". This statement should also be considered obsolete. The fact that a model can continue to exist only shows that some construction path did not stop immediately; it does not show that the distinction between library and ordinary contracts is still correct, much less that Yul identifiers have acquired declaration context they do not otherwise have.

These old examples are retained not to reopen approaches that have already been withdrawn, but because they reflect lines of reasoning that were actually used. If name-based classification, null placeholders, or a unified dictionary are proposed again, first check the reasons given here: format reading, declaration kinds, and name lookup are adjacent concerns, not the same layer.

# Source mapping and fail-high proposal

The previous draft grouped coordinate fields and failure policy into the same set of checks, leaving the scope unclear. This version proposes "test separately, compare at the end": source mapping checks cover only serialization output, and fail-high checks cover only the command-line failure path. That way, even if both come up in the same compatibility review, we won't assume up front that they are handled by the same file or call chain.

### Source mapping examples

Use a newly created empty mapping object as a fixed test case, then prepare another object with a relative filename. Keep the field names and numeric values in the output examples; no additional compatibility-layer fields are needed. The legacy Solidity AST sample should continue to retain `name`, but this is only an observation from the legacy sample and must not be generalized into a universal field for compact AST. The result-filtering example should retain JSON's `description` and leave `performs a multiplication on the result of a division:` unchanged, so field investigation and detector-text investigation don't get mixed together.

There are two candidate approaches on this side. Reusing the existing serialization shape requires few changes, but the examples need to confirm whether the empty object's starting position and the relative filename are stable; adding a compatibility output layer makes migration easier for callers, but creates two sets of fields and is not recommended at this stage.

### fail-high two-state test

With the switch off, the candidate behavior is to retain the existing collection flow; with the switch on, the candidates are to exit immediately on failure, or continue collecting and return a failure at the end. The former exposes failures earlier, at the cost of potentially leaving already collected results without a chance to be output; the latter is less disruptive to callers that read partial results, but makes the failure location less obvious. The available material isn't enough to declare a default behavior.

The test only needs to use the same fixed input and record, for each switch state, the exit status, the stage at which failure text appears, and whether existing results are retained. If the difference is confined to the exit path, the explanation can go near the command-line interface; if it also changes source mapping JSON, return to the previous set of examples and redraw the boundaries.

The direct dependencies of `slither/core/source_mapping/source_mapping.py` can serve as a starting point for investigating Source serialization, but cannot be used to assign an owner for fail-high. In the next draft, decide whether to keep option A based on the actual output.

# Source Mapping and fail-high Proposal

This document has evolved from the original approach of "considering the two compatibility issues together" into two side-by-side trial proposals that do not share implementation assumptions. The earlier assessment is still retained because it explains why the initial investigation treated the source mapping file and the fail-high flag as part of the same line of inquiry; going forward, however, file location is no longer treated as evidence of command-line behavior.

### Trade-offs Left by the Early Draft

v1 favored putting coordinate examples, result text, and the failure flag into a single validation package. The rationale was practical: running a fixed input once would show both JSON and the command-line output. Its problems were equally apparent: if the exit timing changed, caller Fang Ke might see only half the results; if the result description changed, it would be hard to tell whether the change was in the detector output or the serialization path. Another earlier assumption was that `name` could be used directly as a common node label across different forms of AST. That assumption belongs only alongside the old samples and should not become a field guarantee in the new interface.

After the v2 review, the proposals were split. Source mapping retains an empty object, an object with a relative filename, and a legacy AST sample; fail-high uses the same input with the flag in two states, off and on. The split adds one more fixture, but gives each result a narrower scope for interpretation. For now, we are not opting to add compatibility fields, nor are we assigning the implementation of fail-high to `slither/core/source_mapping/source_mapping.py`. This file's currently visible direct neighbors are `re`, `Dict`, `Union`, `Optional`, `List`, `Tuple`, `Context`, and `SlitherCompilationUnit`; this is enough to support local observations of Source object serialization, but not enough to identify the flag's caller.

### Which Set to Try First

First lock down the source mapping output, then try fail-high. The former has a smaller input, and its output can be saved directly; the latter requires saving both the exit status and the results already produced, not just looking at the last line in the terminal. The source mapping fixture must retain at least three things: the empty object's starting position, the relative filename field, and the legacy AST node's `name`. The third item is only to prevent old fields from accidentally being written into the new coordinate protocol; it does not mean that the two types of AST have been unified.

Result investigation continues to use the existing public-facing notation. In the candidate examples, JSON's `description` remains the result description field, and the text `performs a multiplication on the result of a division:` continues to be retained unchanged. They are used to locate the field and the detection result, respectively; the proposal does not require moving this detector text into the source mapping object, nor does it require reworking result deduplication logic for coordinate fields.

The description of current behavior proposed for inclusion in the interface baseline is as follows:

> Source.to_json returns JSON in mapping form for a newly created source mapping, with start set to 0, and exposes filename_relative; result investigation continues to use description and performs a multiplication on the result of a division: as the public-facing search terms. Source mapping JSON uses the start key to represent the mapping's starting coordinate, and a new empty source mapping starts at zero.

This passage specifies only the shape that should be observed in the source mapping examples. It does not determine the default value for fail-high, nor does it state whether failures are always written to the result JSON. If both sides change in the same regression, they must still be assessed separately using their respective examples.

### Candidate Paths for fail-high

Option one is to exit immediately when a failure is detected. Its advantage is that the point of failure is clear, making it suitable for scenarios where callers care only about success or failure; the cost is that detection results already collected may not be output through the existing process. Option two is to finish collecting results and return failure at the end. It preserves more intermediate results, but callers need to distinguish between the two states "results collected" and "process succeeded". There are currently no results from callers that support either option as the default, so this page only recommends experimentation and does not state a final decision.

The two-state experiment uses the same fixed input and records the following for each state: the flag state, the stage at which the failure text appears, the exit status, whether the result JSON exists, and whether existing results remain complete. If only the exit status or exit stage changes, the source mapping protocol does not need to change along with it; if `description`, the coordinate fields, or the way results are retained also change, this cannot be treated as merely a command-line compatibility note. If enabling the flag causes intermediate results that callers rely on to disappear, withdraw the immediate-exit option and keep the end-of-process failure option under review.

### Withdrawal and Open Issues

The source mapping proposal will be withdrawn in either of two cases: a review shows that the empty object's starting position is not produced by Source serialization, or that the relative filename comes from another, unconfirmed entry point. After withdrawal, retain only the observed file navigation and do not add interpretations of the fields. The fail-high proposal will be paused if the outputs for both states cannot be reproduced using the same input; a seemingly complete example must not be used as a substitute for the results.

The default value of fail-high, who generates the failure text, and whether callers rely on results collected before failure remain unresolved. `slither/core/source_mapping/source_mapping.py` remains the entry point for verification on the source mapping side; the actual entry point and owner of the command-line flag are left for the next round of interface review.

# Struct signature and modifier migration notes

Recording signature handling for recursive structs here first. The old path would first fetch the struct fields, then have the surrounding code join them into text; ordinary nested structs didn't show a problem, but there was no explicit stopping point when a field led back to the original struct.

The original idea was to bring signature conversion back to the declaration side. The first place examined was `slither/core/declarations/solidity_variables.py`: declaration objects and type objects sit next to each other here, so we can at least examine "where the fields come from" separately from "where the text continues to be concatenated". The migration doesn't require moving all declaration-related logic into a single function; it only requires that signature termination checks not be scattered across the surrounding code.

The tentative approach at the time was to return only the struct name when conversion encountered the same struct again. Arrays, scalars, and tuple positions would still be preserved by the outer layer. This was a working hypothesis, not a confirmed formatting rule; we need to find a genuinely self-referential input and confirm that, once expansion stops at the name, the surrounding code hasn't scrambled the field order or misplaced parentheses.

Start by trying the following in order:

1. Keep the old caller and feed the new conversion entry point a field that leads back to an already visited struct.
2. Keep both the old and new outputs; don't use a visual "looks unchanged" check as the pass criterion.
3. Check whether the caller is still filling in struct fields; if it is, the stopping point hasn't actually moved into the conversion process.
4. Track modifier identifier path separately. It's also close to the declaration objects, but it shouldn't be treated as a byproduct of recursive signature handling just because it's in the same batch of changes.

When restoring the old path, first let the caller continue to use the original field expansion result. Don't maintain both old and new copies of the field state on the declaration object at the same time; otherwise, it will be hard to tell which path the text came from on the next rollback.

# Structural Signature and modifier Migration Notes

## Legacy Reasoning Retained

The initial implementation split the problem in two: once conversion encountered an already-seen structure, it returned the name; the caller filled in array markers, scalar fields, and parentheses based on its position. This was a small change at the time, and it also made a simple self-referential sample stop expanding.

After review, this split is no longer suitable as a migration approach. Signature text is not a handful of field fragments that can be concatenated at will. If a caller receives only the name, it has to guess whether it represents an array element, a regular field, or a tuple member; different callers may also start recording "seen structures" at different times. On ordinary structures, the two paths can easily produce the same text; mutual references are what expose the inconsistent boundaries.

The legacy convention remains on this page because old callers may still consume partial fragments. It can be used to observe old behavior, but it must no longer define the format of the new path.

## Start with the Surrounding Declarations

The current reference point is still `slither/core/declarations/solidity_variables.py`. The file-visible direct dependencies include `Context`, `CustomError`, `ElementaryType`, and `TypeInformation`. These names show that context, error declarations, and type information all exist near the declaration layer; not all of these objects need to be touched in this migration.

Only two things need to be checked here: whether the structure and its field types come from the same declaration state; whether signature conversion handles the recursion boundary and field syntax internally. If the latter is true, the caller then consumes only the complete result, rather than taking over a piece of type text that still needs to be completed.

The early sketch is below; the second flow is what this change is consolidating:

```text
Old: field declaration -> caller records seen name -> partial fragment -> outer concatenation
New: declaration and field types -> signature conversion entry point -> complete text
```

This is not a runtime call graph. It only identifies which side is responsible for the termination state and type syntax. In the old diagram, the collector knows when to stop, but the concatenator does not know whether a complete type has been formed after stopping; after migration, both decisions should be made within the same conversion flow.

## A Revised Position After Review

The rule "Return the name when a repeated structure is encountered for the first time, and let the outer layer fill in the rest" was previously treated as a sufficient fix; it is now explicitly ruled out. The stopping point cannot be determined solely by an outer-layer convention. The conversion entry needs to maintain the state of visited structures and end the current descent when it encounters a repeated structure; array and scalar representations should also be formed within the same conversion flow.

This does not require bringing all type handling near the declaration file into scope. `CustomError` and `Context` can serve as clues for locating object relationships, but there is no evidence that they should participate in recursion termination. Treating all objects adjacent within the file as part of the migration scope would only broaden the change surface and obscure the entry point actually responsible for producing signature text.

Do not limit the comparison to a character-by-character check. The old path may expand fields first and then have the outer layer add array notation or parentheses; if the new path terminates recursion internally, the final text may still be the same, but the intermediate fragments will not correspond one-to-one. Conversely, matching old and new output on a non-recursive sample cannot prove that the stopping position is correct.

Comparison should instead be object-by-object: first confirm that the input actually contains a field leading back to a visited structure; then locate where the stop decision is made; finally check whether arrays and scalars are still represented by the same flow. If the caller is still appending field syntax, take that responsibility back first; do not add another name set in the caller.

## Parallel Check for modifier

The modifier identifier path is a separate track. It and signature conversion both pass through declaration-related objects, but they address different problems: the former is concerned with whether an identifier still yields the expected result after a normal call; the latter with whether type text fully terminates at the recursion boundary.

Therefore, do not record a modifier regression as the conclusion that the signature changes caused it. Successfully getting through the debug entry only shows that the entry is usable; migration verification still requires the return value or raw diagnostic from the ordinary call entry. Without that result, mark it at most as a parallel item pending investigation; a recursive sample cannot substitute for it.

If the same batch of changes affects both paths, first revert their respective call sites separately, then see whether the symptom remains. Collapsing the two changes into a single "declaration-layer regression" will make it impossible to distinguish later whether signature termination is incorrect or the identifier failed to reach the target branch.

## Rollback Draft

An early version only said, "Switch back to the old caller." This is insufficient to restore changes already migrated into the conversion entry. If the new path uses visited-state tracking, rollback must check at least two places: whether the caller still depends on the new conversion result; whether the conversion entry still retains state usage that serves only the new path.

Reverting only the caller-side changes may let the old caller read intermediate information prepared by the new path; reverting only the conversion-side changes will leave the new caller with an incomplete result. Both mixed states make the next comparison meaningless.

Before and after rollback, preserve the same object that triggers the recursion boundary and its corresponding output. If modifier is checked as well, retain that path's return value or diagnostic separately; do not concatenate it with the signature text into a single line. Later review needs to determine at which boundary the object stopped, rather than guessing the input again from the "recursion anomaly" label.

Still needed: minimal self-referential input; the modifier return value or raw diagnostic from the ordinary call entry; a comparison of field order after rollback.

# Struct Signatures and modifier Migration Notes

This entry has remained near the declaration side, not because recursive signatures and modifier identifier path are part of the same failure, but because these two issues appeared one after the other during the same compatibility change. Early investigators saw object names at the same level and easily conflated "stop recursion" and "identifier reachability" into a single check; later records separated them, but did not remove the original mistaken path.

The current search still starts at `slither/core/declarations/solidity_variables.py`. Near that file, you can find `Context`, `CustomError`, `ElementaryType`, and `TypeInformation`. These objects show local adjacency, not a migration ownership table: types, contexts, and declarations are close together in the same place, but this is no basis for asserting that they share caches, stopping state, or recovery switches.

The records below are preserved in the order in which they were left at the time. Some older paragraphs no longer apply, but they explain why responsibility for signature conversion was later brought back to a single entry point, and why the modifier issue was not folded into the same fix along the way.

## 2023-06-26: Initially the Only Goal Was to Stop Expansion

The earliest draft described the symptom narrowly: if a struct field pointed back to the original struct, field expansion would keep descending. At the time, the assumed solution was for the caller to maintain a set of struct names it had already seen; once a name repeated, it would return the name, leaving the outer layer to fill the remaining fields, array markers, and parentheses back into the text.

This assumption came from the simplest form of a self-referential struct. It seemed straightforward on paper: the caller already had the struct name and knew which field it was assembling, so it seemed that all it needed to do was avoid entering that struct again. The initial draft therefore described the migration goal as "the declaration side supplies a stopping fragment, and the outer layer completes the signature".

At the time, modifier identifier path was also placed on the same list of items to investigate. This was only because both issues required looking at declaration objects, not because they had already been observed to share a failure location. The initial draft had neither results from ordinary modifier calls nor raw diagnostics; it was only marked as a path requiring separate investigation.

The old sketch is still retained below:

```text
Declaration fields
   ↓
Caller: set of seen names
   ↓
Local type fragment
   ↓
Caller: fill in fields and text boundaries
```

This diagram is obsolete. This is not because the concept of "seen structs" is itself wrong, but because the scope of the set and the point where the text was closed off were separate. Different calls Fang Ke can begin tracking at different levels, so the same struct could be treated as new or repeated depending on the call order. Signature rules should not be determined by this incidental order of entry.

## Recovery Approach Retained from the Early Stages

The initial draft also suggested: if the new result looked questionable, simply switch back to the old caller. At the time, this suggestion applied to an experiment that had not yet been moved out of the outer layer, because state still lived on the calling side. It did not account for the situation where visitation state had already moved into the conversion process after the migration was complete.

This section is being kept to remind maintainers of the old branch: old callers once expected partial fragments, not complete types. If you see the surrounding code still appending array notation or field boundaries on the old branch, do not immediately change it to the current form; first confirm whether that call path has actually been migrated. The old output can show what historical callers consumed, but it cannot automatically serve as the definition of the new format.

## 2024-04-16: The review addendum shifted responsibility

During the second revision, the review did not accept the claim that "when a duplicate name is encountered, leave it to the outer layer." The problem was not the act of returning a name, but that the outer layer did not know whether it had received a complete type expression or a fragment that still needed further interpretation.

Structure fields may appear in different syntactic positions. If one caller handles array wrapping, another handles joining fields, and a third handles tuple boundaries, the remaining formatting responsibilities after recursion stops will vary by caller. For ordinary nested structures, this division of work may happen to produce the same text; for mutually referencing structures, a missing or extra layer somewhere is not easy to locate.

After this review, the working conclusion changed to: visited-structure state and recursion stopping boundaries should be managed at the signature conversion entry point; the same process must also preserve the representation of fields in array, scalar, or composite positions. Callers no longer interpret the internal structure of the return value and receive only the completed signature text.

This is a shift in responsibility, not a requirement to move all type-related logic near the file into the declaration module. `Context`, `CustomError`, `ElementaryType` and `TypeInformation` are still merely neighboring objects encountered during investigation. The existing material does not support including all of them in the scope of the recursive signature implementation.

The margin of the review page also contained a more forceful proposal: "The declaration layer's cache should serve both signatures and modifier." This was not adopted later. Although the two paths are adjacent, there is no evidence that they share the same kind of state; coupling them would only make an identifier regression look like a signature termination failure.

## An inadequate comparison method

At one point, someone tried comparing the old and new output character by character, assuming that the migration could be accepted if the text matched. This method was not retained as a verification criterion.

The old path may first expand the fields, with the surrounding code then appending array notation or parentheses; if the new path terminates recursion and completes the field representation at the conversion entry point, the final text may match, but the intermediate fragments have no correspondence at all. Comparing only the final strings for equality cannot show that the stopping point has been moved out of the caller.

Conversely, identical output for non-recursive structures is also of no value. It only shows that the two paths happen to be compatible on inputs without back edges; it cannot verify who is responsible for ending the descent after an already visited structure is encountered. The comparison was later split into three questions: whether the input actually contains a back edge; whether the decision to stop occurs during conversion or in the caller; whether arrays and scalars are still represented by the same conversion process after stopping.

This experiment record was not expanded into a unified test table. It only ruled out a comparison method that would mislead migration decisions. If subsequent samples report only "the text is the same," the three points above still need to be checked again.

## Boundaries of the old approach

The old approach was attractive because it required few changes: each call site kept a set of names, repeated names were output directly, and the call site continued concatenating the subsequent text as usual. It did indeed keep one or two self-referential samples from recursing indefinitely.

The problem is that the more call sites there are, the more stopping rules there are. One entry point might record a name before entering a field, while another might record a name at an array element; even if both say "already seen," their actual meanings are different. Worse, every call site has to know where the type text should be closed, so the signature format becomes an aggregate of multiple local conventions.

The old approach is no longer used for new migrations, nor is it the long-term path after a rollback. It can still serve as an object of observation: if an old call path outputs a local fragment, that indicates the path has not yet completed its migration of the consumption boundary; if a new call path is still adding field syntax at the outer layer, the conversion entry point's responsibilities have not been fully consolidated.

## 2025-10-01: Field notes on the recursive sample

When processing of SLT-204 began, the record noted that one point in "recursive structure signature termination" was still unconfirmed. The notes left afterward did not describe it as a global signature failure; instead, they pointed out that this input and output remain in detection result JSON and the printer's text snapshot. This scope is important: the available material supports finding a short example among existing samples, but does not support treating all regression corpus as the same problem.

The same record was later completed, but that act of completion itself does not mean that all adjacent issues have been closed. At most, it shows that the work item ended at that time; whether the input can pass through conversion again and whether the stopping point is still at the same level must still be verified against the retained output.

The practical procedure here is not to expand the sample set first, but to first find, among existing regressions, the shortest object that loops back to an already visited structure. Ordinary deep nesting is not recursion. Only when a field truly loops back to a structure that has already been visited can the stopping semantics be checked; bringing in samples with no back edge will only make both the old and new paths appear normal on the surface.

For this object, first obtain the signature conversion result, then check whether the outer layer is still adding type syntax. If the caller continues to append array markers, tuple boundaries, or structure fields, the migration is not complete. At this point, do not add a second-layer "seen" check to the caller; that will only bury the old division of responsibilities deeper.

## 2025-10-08: Gaps that remain after the completion record

After the status of SLT-204 was changed to complete, this page did not remove the earlier stopping rules. The reason is not to endorse the old implementation, but that the completion record and the migration boundary are not the same thing. The old rules can explain the source of some surrounding text, and can also explain why a later rollback could not remove only one call site.

The gap left at the time was whether the shortest real example could pass through the same transformation again, and whether the detection result JSON and the output in the printer's text snapshot both pointed to the same stopping position. Without these two objects, do not use "completed" in place of concrete input and output.

This is also the minimum scope for comparing the old and new paths. The comparison only needs the same object that triggers the back edge, the old-path output, and the new-path output; there is no need to include unrelated declaration objects as well. The signature result being close to other declaration capabilities does not mean they should be modified together in this check.

## 2025-10-29: the modifier regression was not folded into the signature conclusion

SLT-221 recorded a regression in the modifier identifier path result after the upgrade and was blocked at the time because the on-call colleague for Solidity AST Parsing was unavailable. This status did not provide the final resolution branch, nor did it explain that the recursive signature was the root cause.

Therefore, this page only retains it as a parallel migration check. It must go through a user's normal invocation, rather than only through the debug entry point; the return value or original diagnostic should be retained. A debug entry point succeeding at most shows that the entry point did not fail immediately; it cannot replace the result of a normal invocation.

There was a natural but incorrect idea: since modifier and signature can both be looked up starting from a declaration object, identifier resolution should also be moved into the signature changes. This idea was abandoned. The signature track focuses on whether the type text can terminate at the back edge, while the modifier track focuses on whether an identifier path reaches a result. The two cannot share a single "fixed" conclusion.

If both tracks change after the same batch of changes, first remove their respective call sites separately and leave their respective outputs. On the signature side, a structural object that triggers the back edge can be used for comparison; on the modifier side, wait for the concrete result or diagnostic from a normal invocation. Without the latter, do not specify which resolution branch should be reverted.

## 2025-11-05: what returning to the backlog means

SLT-221 was later returned to the backlog because it fell out of sync with the release window. This action should be read as meaning that the work was not continued to closure at that time; it should not be read as meaning that the problem had disappeared, nor should it be taken to imply that the signature migration had been proven unrelated.

This page therefore retains a narrow recovery principle: restore the signature transformation according to the known responsibility boundaries; keep modifier on its original path until a concrete result from a normal invocation is obtained. Rolling back the unknown identifier branch together with the known recursive boundary would re-entangle the two problems.

For the signature path, when preparing a rollback, split the change between the caller side and the conversion side. The caller side no longer depends on the new conversion result, and the conversion side likewise does not retain visited-state handling used only by the new path. If only one half can be rolled back, do not mark that state as recovered: the old callFang Ke can read the new state, and new callers may also read incomplete text.

The recovery record should at minimum retain a single shared input, the output from each of the two paths, and whether the modifier's routine entry point was checked in the same pass. That way, the next person handling it can replay the specific differences rather than start over from "recursive exception" and guess the object again.

## The actual sequence during migration

Migration does not mean replacing every field expansion with a new formatting function. First inspect the call sites that consume the signature result: if they depend on local fragments, first reduce the consumption boundary to "obtain the complete signature"; then move visited state, termination checks, and field expressions into the conversion entry point.

Proceed in the following order:

1. Choose an object one of whose fields leads back to an already visited structure, and mark the back edge in the record. Do not use ordinary nesting in its place.
2. Obtain the result from signature conversion, and check whether termination is determined by the conversion flow rather than by the caller-maintained set of names.
3. Check whether array and scalar representations still remain in the same conversion result. If the caller continues appending field syntax, stop expanding the migration scope for now.
4. Use the old path as an observation-only baseline. The old output is only for identifying differences, not for redefining the new format.
5. Check modifier identifier path separately through the routine call, and save the return value or raw diagnostic; treat the debug entry result as a separate reference.
6. If either path produces an unstable result, retain the input, path, and output first, then decide whether to roll back. A "regression" without these artifacts cannot be pinpointed.

The responsibility mapping can be abbreviated as:

```text
Before migration
Caller ──maintains visited structure──> Local fragment ──concatenates──> Text

After migration
Caller ──requests signature──> Conversion entry
                              ├─Visited state
                              ├─Recursive termination boundary
                              └─Field syntax expression
                                           ↓
                                        Complete text

Parallel check
Routine call ──> modifier identifier path ──> Return value or raw diagnostic
```

The arrows indicate responsibility ownership, not that every object is invoked one by one during a single run according to the diagram. In particular, the parallel check should not be appended to the end of signature conversion; it is merely another path whose result needs to be saved separately as part of the same compatibility check.

## Scope limitations left by the review

One review proposed that, because the declaration file interacts with multiple type objects at once, all type handling could be consolidated here. That proposal did not become part of the migration scope on this page. The current material only supports checking termination for recursive structure signatures, the representation of arrays and scalars, and the results of routine modifier calls.

There is likewise no evidence that expression rendering and structure signatures share a formatting entry point. Both generate text, but textual adjacency alone is not enough to assume shared state. This question is being set aside, to be handled separately if an explicit call relationship is found later.

The review also confirmed the rollback boundaries: the signature track can be rolled back based on the division of responsibilities between the conversion entry point and its callers; the modifier track lacks sufficient evidence to specify a rollback point on the parsing side. If both tracks change in the same release, record two observations, rather than letting one conclusion cover the other.

## 2026-02-23: Current Compatibility Criteria

The earlier legacy proposals, on-call logs, and unfinished modifier samples are retained here to clarify the responsibility boundaries for the current requirements. When checking recursive structures now, it is no longer acceptable for callers to fill in the remaining signature fragments after processing stops; the conversion entry point must deliver a complete, consumable result.

Recursive struct signature conversion must terminate and normalize a structure containing an unsized St array and a uint256 field to (St[],uint256); the public compatibility example for adjacent expression rendering is (1,None). Solidity signature conversion for recursive structs preserves nested unsized arrays and scalar fields in canonical form. The string representation of a tuple expression preserves element order and renders empty elements as None.

These criteria are limited to the results of recursive structure signature conversion and adjacent expression rendering. They do not place modifier identifier path under the same rule, nor do they require inferring the same behavior for all adjacent objects visible from `slither/core/declarations/solidity_variables.py`.

Once the current migration is complete, callers should request only complete signatures. If callers are found to still append array brackets, tuple boundaries, or struct fields, first restore the state from before responsibilities were consolidated and identify the consumption boundary, rather than masking the problem with additional name sets.

## Items Not Yet Split Off

Among the materials left by SLT-204, the detection result JSON and the printer's text snapshots remain the starting points for further cross-checking. The next pass should first select the shortest genuine recursive example from these, then check whether the result can be converted again. Do not start by expanding to the entire regression corpus.

SLT-221 still lacks return values or raw diagnostics from users' routine calls. It was once blocked and was then moved back to the backlog; none of these historical statuses constitutes a final conclusion. When signature conversion has been checked against the boundaries on this page, the result for modifier should still be kept separate.

Another unresolved point is whether expression rendering and structural signatures share a formatting entry point. The existing records only state that their textual results need to be checked separately, and do not establish whether the changes should be combined.

## Old appendix: Purpose of the quick patch

The quick patch once recommended was: each caller maintains a set of names, outputs the name when it encounters a duplicate, and then continues adding array and field syntax itself. This patch is no longer used for new migrations.

It once helped confirm that "continuing to drill down" is not acceptable, so it is retained as a counterexample for pinpointing the issue; however, it spreads the definition of when to stop and type closure across multiple call sites. If an old branch still retains this handling, do not casually clean it up to mask the differences. First perform an explicit comparison using the old path, then schedule its removal separately.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Contract Declarations and pedantic

First, separate reports by the reported entry point. Don't put observations about public contract declarations and pedantic results in the same record.

```text
Compatibility issue
├─ Contract declaration or library-related behavior observed
│  └─ Check slither/core/declarations/contract.py first
└─ pedantic default value or package version mismatch observed
   └─ Save the entry point, terminal output, and installed package information
```

## Declaration Side

The earlier investigation started in the declarations directory. This section records issues like "Public Contract Declarations and library Flag"; not every contract model issue needs to be closed out here.

First, clearly record which object the report refers to: whether it is a regular contract declaration or a declaration being treated as a library, and whether the issue occurs when reading the declaration or later when a caller uses the object. The two symptoms can look very similar in the terminal; don't put them in the same branch based on keywords alone.

The quick heuristic used at the time was: if the declaration object could be retrieved, investigate the library angle later. This was intended to reduce the amount of initial troubleshooting; it did not cover cases where the caller still handled the object as a different kind of contract. For reports like this, retain the original object name and entry point; don't replace them with a generic "compatibility failure".

Near the file, you can see `logging`, `Path`, type annotations, and references to compilation platform types. On the first pass, note only these neighboring items; don't infer where the library logic lives from the import list. If you can't find the object name from the report in the file, stop there on the declaration side and check what object the caller received; don't keep guessing based on the directory layout.

## pedantic and Package Information

For the other branch, start from the entry point the user used. Save the terminal output first, then check the workspace for visible side effects. Output saying the default value is wrong doesn't mean the installed package is also wrong; the same applies in reverse.

The old notes treated "being able to reproduce the pedantic message" as a sign that the package version had switched. Treat that only as a working hypothesis from that time. During troubleshooting, the entry point, output, and package information should still be recorded side by side; if any one is missing, don't classify the issue as a version problem.

Stop conditions:

- On the declaration side, only the object's source has been confirmed, not how it is used afterward;
- On the pedantic side, there is only the message text, with no installed package information;
- Records from the two branches were mixed together in the same test, making it impossible to tell which input triggered the behavior.

In these cases, leave the records as they are and wait for the next result that can be verified.
