# Contract Declarations and pedantic Troubleshooting Tree

This old record originally split 2026.09-compat anomalies into two branches: on one side, callers treated a public contract declaration as a library; on the other, pedantic Default Configuration and Package Version appeared inconsistent. On-site errors usually present as only one brief symptom, but the investigator first has to decide whether to start from the declaration object or the user entry point.

The tree from the early days is still below. It was once used for on-call handoffs; its branch saying "if the declaration is retrievable, investigate it first and defer library" later proved overly optimistic, but was not removed from the record.

```text
Compatibility anomaly appears
├─ See a contract declaration or library-related symptom
│  ├─ Start by examining slither/core/declarations/contract.py
│  ├─ Distinguish the declaration object from where that object is subsequently used
│  └─ Old judgment: when the object can be retrieved, the library branch can be deferred
└─ See a pedantic default value or package-version mismatch
   ├─ Record the actual entry point
   ├─ Record the terminal output
   └─ Record the post-install package information and workspace side effects
```

The tree's purpose is only to keep on-call staff from writing the two types of symptoms in the same conclusion. It is not a complete module-by-module call graph, nor does it cover all compatibility issues. If a report contains both a declaration object and a strict-mode notice, first open a record for the earliest observable symptom; retain the other item as a parallel clue, and do not immediately write it as the cause.

## Initial Handling Approach

The first stop for the declaration side has always been `slither/core/declarations/contract.py`. Descriptions received at the time were often written as "Public Contract Declarations and library Flag", but this phrase itself did not indicate whether the problem occurred during object creation, property access, or caller classification. The old procedure required recording these three points separately first:

- Which declaration object entered this path;
- Where the library determination in the report came from;
- Whether the observer saw the discrepancy while reading the object or after using it.

These three locations cannot be interchanged. If a record only says "the library flag is problematic," later investigators often search the declaration directory directly, then project the caller's classification discrepancy back onto the object itself. The original records did not contain enough evidence to prove that every discrepancy came from the declaration model, so they did not assign a single uniform cause.

At the time, inspecting this file directly showed `logging`, `Path`, several type annotations, and references to the compiler-platform type. They only indicated that these items were adjacent to the file; they did not show that any import was responsible for library classification. Some early investigators treated the import list as the troubleshooting order and first expanded the investigation through type annotations and path objects; this made the investigation sprawl and still did not bridge the reported object and the actual use site.

Older handoff notes often say "Start with declarations". The actionable meaning of this sentence should be narrower: first open the declaration file and confirm that the report actually concerns a public contract declaration; if you cannot find the reported object or connect it to the reported behavior, stop here. Do not assume that all subsequent logic is in the same file just because the directory name contains declarations.

### Retained earlier assessment

> As long as the public declaration object can be obtained, the library branch can wait; first establish whether the declaration path can be entered.

This was a working assessment in the initial draft, retained to explain why some older records lack a review of the library side. It conflated "the object can be obtained" with "the caller classifies the object as expected". During later reviews, this shortcut proved insufficient to explain the results from callers that were still using the object, so it can no longer be treated as an exclusion criterion.

However, this page did not establish a new unified replacement criterion. When handling similar reports, continue to retain two observations: whether the object enters the declaration path, and whether the caller uses it in the same entry-point invocation. If either observation is missing, the conclusion can only be recorded as unconfirmed; the other observation cannot be used to fill the gap.

## Declaration-side triage branches

Start with the reported object, not with the word "compatibility".

### The report explicitly mentions public contract

First confirm whether the object the reporter refers to is a public contract declaration. Do not include every contract-related name that appears in the source file in the record. Retain only the objects actually reached by the entry point and the locations where they were observed.

If the object can be located on the declaration side, the next step is to check whether the description of the abnormal behavior is still confined to reading declarations. If the message appears only after the object is passed to subsequent logic, the declaration-side record should say "Object is present, use site not verified", rather than "Declaration side is normal". The former preserves the boundary needed for the next step, while the latter can mislead people into thinking that the library branch has been ruled out.

If the object cannot be matched to the report on the declaration side, stop guessing further. Return to the entry point and fill in which object name the report uses, where the object was obtained, or whether similar names were simply treated as the same object. The initial draft grouped declarations with similar names into the same category on several occasions, and there is no subsequent material from which to reconstruct those cases, so that approach must not be copied.

### The report calls the object a library

First record where the object is "called a library". This may be in the user's description, terminal output, or the classification reflected in the caller's behavior when handling the object; these three kinds of material cannot be treated as the same evidence.

The old manual tended to ask "Is the flag set?" first. This question leans too heavily toward speculation about the implementation. A more useful question during triage is: at what point does this entry point use the object as a library? If all you know is that the object comes from the declaration layer, but you do not know where it is used, the library branch can only remain pending investigation.

Early records treated "the object can be obtained through the public declaration path" as positive evidence for classification as a library. That wording is no longer appropriate. Public declarations, object availability, and library classification are not observations at the same level; compressing them into one sentence makes it impossible for later reviews to identify which level is missing.

### Only directory clues remain

Sometimes a record contains only a file path and a vague issue name. Do not expand this into a full investigation. The minimum entry to retain is: the issue name points to the declaration path, but the actual object and its use site have not yet been obtained. This prevents the file location from being mistakenly recorded as a conclusion next time.

If someone asks for a library result based directly on a path, stop here. A file path is an entry point for reading, not a classification result. A few quick replies in older versions did not follow this rule, and the original situation was not fully documented later either.

## The pedantic branch starts at the user's entry point

The starting point for this branch is not the declaration file, but the entry point the user actually uses. The creation description for SLT-225 requires running through the usual entry point and keeping separate records of the terminal output and workspace side effects; this requirement is stated separately because past records often excerpted just one line of a message and then interpreted it as a package version change.

First, divide the material into two columns:

| Captured at the time | What cannot be inferred directly from it |
| --- | --- |
| The entry point the user actually used | All environments use the same default configuration |
| Terminal output | The installed package has definitely changed |
| Workspace side effects | The message is definitely caused by package metadata |
| Package information | That entry point necessarily reads the same configuration |

The right-hand column of the table does not contain conclusions, just boundaries that older records repeatedly crossed. When a pedantic message appears, the message text itself only shows that this particular invocation of the entry point produced that text; to discuss the default configuration, at minimum the entry point and package information must also be included in the same record.

### Output before interpretation

Older handling typically started by excerpting terminal output into the issue description, then adding "the defaults changed" or "the package was not updated" from memory. This sequence left quite a few conclusions that cannot be verified. A more workable sequence would be to first preserve the full range of output, then separately record the entry point used for the run and the workspace side effects.

"Workspace side effects" here refers to the visible results actually left, or not left, in the workspace after a run. These and the terminal text are two different kinds of records: the former should not be reduced to "success" or "failure", and the latter should not be replaced with a summary of the side effects. Without these two separate observations, it is not possible to determine later whether the discrepancy arose in the entry point, configuration reading, or information about the installed package.

If all you have is one message line containing pedantic, do not add a version-based explanation yet. Preserve that line's location within the output, and request the missing entry point information. If you have package information but no output, do not work backward to infer whether that run triggered a strict failure either; package information is only material from the installation side.

### The old attribution shortcut

The initial draft used the following simplification:

> When a pedantic message appears, start by treating it as a mismatch between the installed package version and the default configuration.

This is a historical approach, and should not be treated as the first conclusion in current troubleshooting. It omitted preserving the entry point and workspace results, causing the same kind of message to be grouped under different version anomalies. This passage is retained so that people reading old tickets can understand why some entries only include terminal excerpts.

A subsequent review did not rewrite that judgment as a new global rule, but only added a narrower requirement: keep separate records of the terminal output and workspace side effects. This requirement does not guarantee that the source of the issue will be identified, but it can prevent a single message from replacing both kinds of material.

### Missing package information

If both the entry point and output are available, but information about the installed package is missing, the record should stop at "Default configuration behavior remains to be checked against package information". Do not write "the package version is abnormal", and do not write "the package version is normal" either. Both statements treat material that has not been collected as known facts.

If package information is available but the entry point has only been relayed verbally, fill in the entry point first. Different entry points may produce different results with the same installation state; after the old documentation mixed them together, subsequent staff could no longer reproduce the original behavior. There is no requirement here to invent commands just to reproduce it, only to record a description of the entry point actually used at the time.

If terminal output and workspace side effects point in different directions, retain both observations. Do not choose one as the "real result" and delete the other. Older records have rewritten runs with no side effects as "no anomalies", which loses the fact of the mismatch with the output.

## When Both Branches Appear

Reports about public contract declarations and the default pedantic configuration sometimes come from the same compatibility check, but this does not mean there is a direct causal relationship between them. The processing order can follow the tree below:

```text
Two types of clues appear in the same entry-point run
├─ Object/declaration-side descriptions come first
│  ├─ Record the object, where it was observed, and whether the declaration path was entered
│  └─ Put pedantic output in a separate paragraph, and do not use it to explain library
├─ pedantic output comes first
│  ├─ Retain the entry point, output, workspace side effects, and package information
│  └─ Put the declaration object in a separate paragraph, and do not use the messages to explain the object classification
└─ Cannot determine which came first
   └─ Preserve the order of the original material; do not synthesize a single root cause
```

This tree deliberately has no "final root cause" box. The available material only supports preserving the two types of behavior separately, not attributing both to the public declaration model or package configuration. An older version once included the handoff note "check the declarations first, and configuration issues will probably disappear as well"; that was experience-based wording left in to reduce how much the on-duty staff had to read, not a verified recovery action.

### Deprecated Merged Record Format

In the past, one type of entry would read:

> The library flag and the pedantic results are both wrong, so update the package first, then revisit the declarations.

This sentence leaves out the object, entry point, output, and package information all at once, making it impossible to know what actual situation "update the package" referred to. Do not reuse it. If you see an old entry in this format, use it only as a clue, and do not use it as grounds to close a new report.

The reason for keeping an old entry is not that it is still reliable, but that it may contain object names or terminal snippets that no longer appear elsewhere. When reading it, first extract the verifiable observations, while retaining the old attribution as a historical attribution.

## On-Call Addendum

Subsequent cards logged the two tracks separately. SLT-208 went through security triage first and only then moved into the in-progress state; it calls for finding a caller still using "Public Contract Declarations and library Flag" and checking the actual version, entry point, and current result. This action does not assert that any particular caller will definitely reproduce the issue, nor does it provide a final judgment on the library classification.

SLT-225 still had one unconfirmed point after moving into the in-progress state. The description left publicly on that card only states that pedantic Default Configuration and Package Version's actual entry point and sample results do not match, and asks for a run through the commonly used entry point, with terminal output and workspace side effects recorded separately. It does not directly attribute the inconsistency to the installation package, defaults, or declaration model.

These two cards are useful for locating follow-up evidence; they should not be read backwards as endorsing the conclusions of the earlier troubleshooting. In particular, the draft's shortcut phrasing, "a warning means a version problem," is not the same as the layers of evidence the cards require us to retain.

## What to retain when recording

Records on the declaration side can be very brief, but at a minimum separate the object from where it was observed. For example:

```text
Object: some object in a public contract declaration
Observation location: declaration read / subsequent use (choose one of the two; write unknown if unknown)
library clue: from report text / from usage location (choose one of the two; write unknown if unknown)
Result: object is present; classification has not yet been checked
```

Here, "some object" is not a recommendation to replace the real object with a placeholder name. Actual records should retain the object name already present in the report; write unknown only when there is no name. The template merely prevents "declaration object" and "library clue" from being put into the same field.

On the pedantic side, retain four categories of evidence: entry point, output, workspace side effects, and package information. They can be brief pieces of text; they do not need to be reorganized into an environment report. The key is to let later reviewers see which part is missing, rather than hide the gap behind "checked."

```text
Entry point: description of the entry point actually used
Terminal output: retain output connected to the observed behavior
Workspace side effects: actual results left behind after running
Package information: information about the installed packages visible at the time
Tentative assessment: write only what the above evidence supports
```

If the draft's claims that "the version has been switched" and "the default value has changed" are not accompanied by this evidence, they should continue to be treated as historical assessments. Do not rewrite them as facts when citing old records, and do not omit the current entry point merely because the text already exists.

## Stop conditions are more important than continuing the search

Stop the current branch in the following situations, and record the gap:

- The declaration file can be opened, but the reported object cannot be matched;
- It is only known that the object comes from a public declaration; its subsequent usage location is unknown;
- There is only the word library, with no context for where it appears;
- There is only a pedantic warning, with no actual entry point;
- There is output but no record of workspace side effects;
- There is package information, but it cannot be determined which run it corresponds to;
- The two types of clues come from different contexts but have been merged into a single incident.

Stopping does not mean renaming the issue "pending confirmation." It should clearly state which object the current work has stopped at: for example, "the declaration object is visible, but the caller's usage location has not been obtained," or "the terminal warning has been retained, but information about installed packages has not been retained." This wording lets the next review fill the missing item directly, rather than restart the entire troubleshooting process.

Conversely, the following are insufficient to move forward: similar object names, directory locations, a standalone strict-mode warning, and version conclusions unsupported by evidence in historical records. They can be kept as search terms, but should not be used for attribution.

## Still-referenced old paragraphs

### Old step A: Update first, then re-verify

An old document once recommended handling the installation package first when a pedantic symptom appeared, then returning to the entry point for verification. That step assumed that all warnings were triggered by changes on the package side. Existing records contain no continuous evidence trail supporting this assumption, so this passage is no longer suitable as the default action.

It is still retained because a few old tickets contain only the wording "the behavior was different after updating." At most, that sentence shows that the observations before and after were different; without the original entry point, output, and package information, it cannot show what caused the change.

### Old step B: A retrievable declaration rules out library
Old Step B treated the ability to obtain the object as the postcondition for the library branch. It did not record when the caller uses the object, nor did it distinguish between "appearing on the declaration side" and "appearing on the classification side". When handling new reports, do not continue to use this step to close the library branch.

Old Step B has not been replaced with "Every object must undergo a full call-chain check" either. # TypeAlias and Literal Migration Notes

This page is still used to look up two old issues: TypeAlias Constants at Assignment Boundaries, and Decimal Literal Text Normalization. It is no longer suitable as a map of implementation responsibilities. The original assessment assigned responsibility for both issues to `tmp_new_elementary_type.py`, which made for easy reading, but a later review found that this was only an entry point for investigation, not enough to establish that the conversion was completed here.

The file is still worth opening from here. The path is `slither/slithir/tmp_operations/tmp_new_elementary_type.py`, and only two adjacent objects are visible:

```python
from slither.slithir.operations.lvalue import OperationWithLValue
from slither.core.solidity_types.elementary_type import ElementaryType
```

These two import statements indicate that both the assignment result and the elementary type should be watched during inspection; they do not establish where TypeAlias is expanded, nor at which layer Literal text is rewritten. The old records treated this adjacency as causation, and that route is preserved below so that readers still arriving via old links know at which step to stop.

## The old route, no longer used as a basis for assessment

The sequence in the initial draft was: find the issue name by searching for "TypeAlias constant" or "decimal Literal", proceed to the temporary operation, and upon seeing `ElementaryType`, classify the issue as elementary type processing; if the examples changed, record both kinds of changes together in the same place. The advantage of this sequence was speed, but the disadvantage was that it conflated "passing through this object" with "being completed in this object".

The advice at the time was also to go straight back to the old path if there was a mismatch. Here, the "old path" meant continuing to trace back to this file using the issue name and call name, not reverting a confirmed implementation change. This wording later caused a misunderstanding: some readers thought the page provided a patch that could be reverted, when what it actually left was a manual investigation route.

The old route is preserved below:

```text
Issue name
  └─ tmp_new_elementary_type.py
       ├─ OperationWithLValue
       └─ ElementaryType
```

It is now only suitable for answering "where to look first", not "where to make changes". If all that is needed is to check historical examples, it can still be used to narrow the reading scope; once the actual processing location for alias constants or decimal text needs to be determined, the investigation cannot end at this diagram.

## Post-migration inspection order

The new recording approach starts by saving the two examples separately. One example covers only the TypeAlias constant at the assignment boundary, while the other covers only the text of a decimal Literal. Do not start by combining them into a single "type compatibility" case; appearing in the same round of compatibility checks does not mean they share a processing chain.

The first step is to clearly document the input to be examined. For an alias constant, record the fact that it appears at the assignment boundary, along with the result from that particular example. For a decimal Literal, record the original text and the observed textual form. The existing material does not provide complete examples or fixed outputs, so this old page does not invent values, type names, or error messages to fill the gaps. This will not make the investigation more automated, but it can avoid the old page's leap from a filename directly to responsibility for conversion.

In the third step, when comparing results, do not use "looks the same" as the pass condition. For alias constants, the type information before and after the same assignment boundary must remain identifiable; for a decimal Literal, the textual forms before and after text normalization must remain comparable. Here, "identifiable" and "comparable" are minimum requirements for the check records, not a promise covering all IR representations. The current material does not provide more detailed equivalence rules, so do not expand these two statements into global criteria for type comparison.

The fourth step is to mark the branches in the records. If the alias-constant example changes but the decimal text does not, place it on the assignment-boundary side and continue investigating; if the text changes but the alias-constant example does not, initially retain it as an observation on the Literal-text side. If both change at the same time, first preserve the two inputs and results separately, rather than using a single modification to explain both changes. The old page equated "happening at the same time" with "having the same cause", and that has been discarded.

```text
Old records: Issue name ──> Temporary operation ──> Assess together

Current checks:
TypeAlias constant example ──> Assignment-boundary record ──> Then inspect temporary-operation adjacency
Decimal Literal text ─> Text record     ──> Then inspect temporary-operation adjacency
```

The two lines in the diagram converge at "inspect temporary-operation adjacency", but their conclusions do not merge. This preserves the convenience of the old entry point without implying that the same object is responsible for both issues.

The initial draft described `tmp_new_elementary_type.py` as "the true entry point for TypeAlias constants". This does not mean that the two issues are unrelated to this path. They remain on this page because this path has consistently been the first place opened, and the adjacency between the assignment lvalue and the elementary type is useful when examining a case. Object: TypeAlias constant
```text
Location: Assignment boundary
Input: [Keep the original example]
Result: [Keep the observed result]
Temporary-operation adjacency: Reviewed / Not reviewed
Notes: [If the result changes, specify which review the change occurred in]

Object: Decimal Literal
Location: Text normalization observation
Input text: [Keep the original text]
Result text: [Keep the observed result]
Failure text or output bytes: [Attach if available]
Temporary-operation adjacency: Reviewed / Not reviewed
```

This is not a new test fixture definition, just a way to avoid squeezing two kinds of material into a single sentence when migrating old records. In particular, do not change "Not reviewed" to "Unrelated": not reviewed means that this entry point was not followed further this time, and does not establish whether responsibility lies inside or outside the file.

If only one of the examples is available for the case, it is fine to fill in only half. In the old records, trying to reach conclusions on both items at once often meant that neither had enough input preserved. It is now preferable to leave the other section blank. For a decimal Literal, the original text is more valuable than the general description "decimal format"; for a TypeAlias constant, the context in which the assignment boundary appears is more valuable than an alias name alone.

## Mapping to cards

SLT-209 preserves the reported issue that "the actual entry point for TypeAlias Constants at Assignment Boundaries does not match the example results". It is suitable for returning to this page with a specific mismatch, not for copying this page's old conclusions back to the card. The card later went through failure_classified and work_started; these statuses only show that work had started, and cannot substitute for example records.

SLT-226 is a user-reported regression supplement for Decimal Literal Text Normalization. The card's to-do explicitly calls for adding repository tests based on the examples reported by the user and preserving the current failure text or output bytes. Its scope was later confirmed and work began, but this page has received no material from which a fixed output could be documented. Therefore, this page only retains the entry point for adding examples, rather than misrepresenting "work has started" as "normalization is complete".

Both cards can be opened at the same time because they were filed under the same compatibility check; when filling them out, continue to keep the two records above separate. If a review only involves SLT-209, there is no need to add Literal content just to make the page complete; the reverse is also true.

When you need to reproduce the old way of reading the page, start with the issue name or call name and go to `slither/slithir/tmp_operations/tmp_new_elementary_type.py`, confirming only the direct adjacency between this file and `OperationWithLValue`, `ElementaryType`. Next, take one example currently on hand and state whether it concerns an alias constant's assignment boundary or a text observation for a decimal Literal. If the input and result are still missing at this point, stop at "Entry point reviewed".

Only when both the example and result have been preserved should you proceed to compare the differences between two checks. If the difference is only in the text, the old route cannot be used to conclude that the TypeAlias side has changed; if the difference is only at the assignment boundary, the old route likewise cannot be used to conclude that text normalization has changed. The purpose of restoring the old reading route is to explain where the old records came from, not to restore the old attribution.

# Decisions on Dependency Filtering and Function Paths

This page originally brought together two neighboring issues: why dependency results are duplicated, and where results should obtain their paths when top-level functions do not belong to a contract. The subsequent review did not combine them into a generic output-cleanup operation. Both affect the final list of findings, but they operate on different objects, and combining them too early would erase distinctions needed during investigation.

The review still starts at `slither/core/slither_core.py`. The directly adjacent items at the top of the file are `json`, `logging`, `os`, and `pathlib`. These are enough to continue investigating result handling and path handling near the same local entry point, but not enough to prove that all callers use the same path. The old investigation notes point here through issue names and call names, so this entry point is retained; the import list has not been presented as evidence of where the implementation belongs.

## Two Branches Retained from the Initial Draft

The early notes first drew a very narrow distinction: duplicates in dependency results should be identified after the results have been formed; paths for top-level functions should start from the top-level declarations themselves. The initial draft did not provide a formula for the fields or establish path strings as a new specification. It only ruled out two convenient but risky shortcuts: deduplicating directly during dependency traversal, and creating an empty contract context for functions that do not belong to a contract.

Both shortcuts appeared to reduce branching at the time. The former moved filtering closer to dependency collection, while the latter allowed reuse of contract-member path handling. The problem is that both collapsed object relationships prematurely. Once only one dependency record remains at the collection stage, there is no way later to tell whether another record was introduced as a duplicate or actually represented a different finding under the same dependency; once a function is placed in an empty contract, there is likewise no way later to distinguish an actual member from a top-level object in a temporary container.

The initial draft therefore did not decide that "all results must be retained" or that "a separate format must be invented for every path". It only retained the necessary context before the determination is made. The same source does not automatically mean the same result, and the presence of a nearby contract declaration does not automatically mean that the function belongs to that contract.

## Where Dependency Results Are Compared

Duplicate Filtering of Dependency Results comes after the results have been formed. The dependency enumeration stage should still retain records produced by inclusion and exclusion until the results themselves can be compared. The reason is specific: the source only indicates where a result entered, not whether two findings express the same thing. If records are collapsed by source during enumeration, the removed record will no longer be visible later, and there will be no way to determine whether instability comes from traversal or result construction.

For result JSON, `description` participates in duplicate-result filtering. It is not merely a note for human readers. Even if two records come from the same dependency, they cannot be merged solely because they share a source if their descriptions refer to different findings; conversely, matching descriptions alone are not sufficient grounds for merging. The current decision only confirms that it must be included in the comparison, without also supplying a fallback key for cases where the description is missing.

Three options for where to do this were compared here. The first was immediate deduplication during dependency traversal. Its advantage is that the change appears small, but its disadvantage is that differences between inclusion and exclusion disappear before result processing begins, making it difficult to look back at why a record appeared when duplicates occur, so this option is not adopted. The second was deduplication based only on the dependency object. It mistakes the same dependency for the same finding and cannot accommodate results from the same source with different descriptions, so it is not adopted either.

The third was comparison after result construction. It preserves the preceding context, at the cost of no longer treating the filtering point as a simple operation on a dependency set. This cost is acceptable because the result layer can at least still see the description and other fields that have already been formed. The decision goes no further than this: it does not authorize collapsing all records with matching descriptions, nor does it authorize falling back to retaining only one record per dependency when a result has a missing field.

Direct checks of the same file tree continue to follow this boundary: first retain inclusion results and exclusion results separately, then observe the findings they produce. Global user configuration must not be changed to manufacture an apparently clean result. When SLT-211 later moves into handoff and handling, this local scope is retained; the cards provide an entry point for reproduction and do not replace the decision here on when filtering occurs.

## Top-Level Function Membership

Top-level function paths are handled separately. Here, a top-level function means a function declaration that does not belong to a contract, not the first function encountered during traversal. Its path starts from its own declaration relationships, and it must not borrow a contract's member path merely because a contract declaration appears nearby in the same file.

Placing all functions with no contract membership into an empty contract was an older option retained during review. It would allow contract members and top-level functions to follow the same branch, but would also conflate actual membership with temporary membership. If downstream code sees only a contract-shaped path, it cannot tell whether that path comes from an actual declaration or from a container added to reuse code. This compatibility cost is not worth hiding with fabricated data.

Another similar fallback is to find the nearest contract declaration. It depends on the traversal position rather than the function's own relationships; when contracts and top-level functions appear in the same source file, traversal order could then change the meaning of the path. This fallback is not adopted either. When there is no contract membership, the result should retain the top-level branch rather than wait for a temporary contract name to wrap it.

This decision does not redefine modifier parsing, visibility filtering for function identifiers, or report text formatting. It only addresses membership: functions that belong to a contract are looked up through member relationships, while functions that do not belong to a contract are looked up through top-level declarations. Callers that accept only member paths need to handle the top-level branch at their own boundaries; the core layer does not fill it in for them using null values or fabricated containers.

## How the Two Tracks Meet

Dependency filtering and top-level paths meet near the final findings, but neither can serve as an upstream substitute for the other. First determine whether a finding belongs to the current file tree or to a dependency, then determine whether the function is a contract member or a top-level function; only after the results have been formed is it possible to examine result fields such as `description` and determine whether the results are duplicates. This way, when a finding is missing, it is at least still possible to distinguish incorrect membership from premature filtering.

This is also why the phrase "unified output cleanup" was not adopted. If top-level functions are first turned into contract members, two originally different function contexts may become similar; if records are first deleted by dependency, there will be no objects left to compare even if the subsequent path determination is correct. The two decisions apply at different boundaries, but both boundaries need to be examined in sequence during review.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Dependency Results" as dependency_result
    state "Top-Level Function Paths" as top_level_path
    state "Output Results" as output_result
    [*] --> dependency_result
    dependency_result --> top_level_path
    top_level_path --> output_result
    output_result --> [*]
```

The order in the diagram is only the observation order used in this review, not a newly added description of the runtime flow. It places dependency records and function membership before result formation and leaves duplicate detection until after output results already exist; it does not turn a missing path into a state that can be silently ignored.

## Boundaries Remaining After the Review

No specific rule filename has been added at this point, and no final list of findings has been fabricated. The evidence needed from the actual environment should show where the top-level declaration enters, the generated function context, and why it cannot be equated with a contract-member result. Only then will subsequent notes add facts rather than substitute an example for the path definition.

A narrower boundary for dependency filtering is still missing: how to handle two records with the same description but different information elsewhere in the results. At this stage, we can only confirm that `description` cannot be removed from the comparison, and that "the same dependency" cannot be used directly as a reason for deletion. This version of the decision likewise does not settle which fallback comparison fields to use when a description is missing.

This version therefore retains two decisions. First, dependency results are formed before duplicate filtering, and `description` is included in the determination. Second, top-level functions retain their own declaration paths and do not obtain member affiliation through the nearest contract or an empty contract. The rule file location, the complete list of findings, and the comparison method for the remaining fields still await the actual review materials needed to fill in the gaps.

# Dynamic Types and Finding Text Proposal

This record remains under the compatibility review entry point, but the two issues were not ultimately handled together as originally planned: dynamic type classification is a matter of tracing through the type layer, while finding text concerns how readers understand the results they receive. They were discussed in the same round mainly because both fell within the regression scope of 2026.09-compat; this does not mean they should share an implementation or validation path.

The investigation initially started at `slither/core/solidity_types/array_type.py`. The direct dependencies visible for that file were `Optional`, `Tuple`, `Literal`, `Expression`, and `Type`. At the time, someone took this as grounds for treating the array-type file as the only place to decide whether a type is dynamic. That entry point can still be used to trace things back, but it does not replace evaluating specific type combinations at the call sites.

## Retained Initial Assessment

The initial draft proposed "centralizing dynamic-type determination in the array-type layer, with callers consuming only the result." The apparent advantage was that changes would be concentrated in one place: array nesting depth, element types, and relationships between adjacent expressions would not have to be handled in multiple places. The trade-offs were not explored at the time. In particular, type aliases, nested arrays, and expressions originating from something other than the array itself could make a single check carry too much semantic weight.

This assessment was retained because old links still bring readers here, but it is no longer the default approach for this round. During review, first distinguish two questions: whether a type should be classified as dynamic, and whether a caller needs only that classification result. The first can be traced through the array-type entry point; the second requires returning to the actual sites that consume the classification result. If both are folded into one boolean check, edge-case types will make it difficult to tell whether the classification or the caller needs to change.

## Two Trial Tracks

The dynamic-type track proposes only two limited options.

- Option A: Continue to use `array_type.py` as the central point for the check, with callers accepting the classification provided by that layer. This makes it easier to revise array-related rules in one place, provided callers do not add differing semantics of their own.
- Option B: Keep that file as an entry point for checking array objects and type relationships, with callers interpreting the classification according to their own use cases. This avoids prematurely pushing unknown expression semantics into type objects, but similar checks may then appear in multiple places.

At the time, there was not enough material to choose between the two. A trial should not stop at "it can return true or false"; it should check whether the same interpretation is required for nested arrays, type aliases, and expression adjacency. If any of these requires bypassing the array-type layer and defining a separate rule, stop treating Option A as a unified way to centralize the rules and record the divergence point, rather than adding another layer of guesswork to `ArrayType`.

The lead on finding text is narrower in scope. SLT-229 points to an obstacle in reading the results after the upgrade: ask readers who were not involved in the changes to follow the instructions and note which pages and links they get stuck on. This cannot prove that the detection logic itself is wrong, nor can it replace a review of the result descriptions. The trial here is to have the description state directly that the multiplication uses the result of a division; the candidate text is `performs a multiplication on the result of a division:`. This text should appear where the function or finding object can supply the context. It must not leave readers with only the detector name to infer the relationship.

The original idea was to treat text formatting as a by-product of the dynamic type classification changes. # Solidity Signature Migration Notes

This record continues from `slither/core/declarations/solidity_variables.py`. The first point found during the walkthrough was the handoff between declaration objects and type objects, with direct dependencies such as `Context`, `CustomError`, `ElementaryType`, and `TypeInformation` nearby. The file's location alone does not establish that all signature rules are implemented here, so for now the migration scope is limited to the stage where "the declaration side passes a type to a caller that needs a Solidity signature".

The earliest draft described the problem as inconsistent name formatting and proposed adding string assembly at each call site. That assessment can now only be retained as a record of the old path. It can easily look fine for simple types, but aliases, arrays, and nested fields cause the "display name" and the "type text in the signature" to diverge. The migration comparison is not about whether a particular name looks better, but whether the same type object goes through the same conversion before being passed downstream.

## Preserve the old results first

Do not start the first batch by changing code. For every declaration that actually passes through a point where a signature is needed, put the following in the same record:

- The object and type category in the declaration;
- The raw string the call site receives through the old path;
- The string produced after switching to centralized conversion;
- The exact location of any difference: the type itself, array markers, nested fields, or extra characters assembled at the call site.

Ordinary elementary type cases are only used to verify the input and output wiring. They do not establish that conversion for aliases, arrays, or structs has passed. If differences appear in the very first group, first return to the input object and the handoff point; do not change the declaration structure and string format at the same time, or it will be impossible to determine which layer changed the result.

`Context` appears among the file's direct dependencies, but there is currently no evidence that it provides the signature format. During migration, initially retain it as a declaration-adjacent dependency, and include this relationship in the samples only if the call path actually obtains type information from the context. Having the conversion read back from the context to reduce parameter passing would broaden the scope of changes and make it impossible to undo only the signature-related changes when restoring the old path.

Keep a separate set of samples for `CustomError`. The parameter types in an error declaration become part of the error signature and cannot be replaced with the result of concatenating ordinary variable names. Error names, parameter names, and source locations are outside the scope of this comparison; here, only check where the parameter types come from, whether they pass through the same conversion point, and whether array or struct fields are still filled in independently by the call site.

## Move from the old path to the new path

The working assumption retained from the old draft is: declaration objects provide local names, and call sites assemble them themselves; error parameters may go through another assembly mechanism. This assumption has not been deleted because it explains why simple samples can pass while complex samples tend to diverge. The new path first retains the type object in the declaration, then forms the type text for Solidity signatures at one explicit point, with callers consuming only that result.

```text
Old path
Declaration object ──Local name──> Call-site assembly
Error parameter ──Local name──> Assembly elsewhere

Migration path
Declaration object ──Type object──> Centralized conversion ──> Call site
Error parameter ──Type object──> Centralized conversion ──> Error signature
```

The two input lines in the diagram represent only the step that requires a signature. It does not mean that variable declarations and error declarations share the entire model, nor does it move `Context`, source mappings, or variable names into type conversion. If an actual walkthrough finds that a category of declarations does not pass through here, note that beside the samples for that category rather than adding an unconfirmed connection just to make the diagram look complete.

## Migrate in batches

### Wire up ordinary types first

Start with a small number of elementary type cases, only confirming that the object received by the conversion entry point has not already been turned into display text by the call site. Record the original and new results, retaining the input category even if the two are identical. Passing here only means that the first section of wiring is stable, not that complex types have been covered.

### Compare aliases separately

Alias samples must record the name the declaration presents to people separately from the type information the signature conversion actually uses. Simple aliases may happen to produce the same text as the underlying type, easily creating the false impression that migration is complete. If the caller still appends a name to the result, first preserve the values before and after the addition side by side, then decide whether to remove that assembly logic; do not hide the difference with a special-case branch.

### Arrays and struct fields

At a minimum, array samples must distinguish between sized and unsized forms, focusing on whether the array markers come from the type's composition or from extra characters supplied by the call site. For struct fields, include samples with bounded nesting. Recursive structures cannot be proven correct through infinite expansion; verify that conversion can terminate at an identifiable recursion point, and preserve the inputs and outputs before and after that level. If the result depends on truncation at the call site, the termination condition is still in the wrong place.

When structs are combined with unsized arrays, do not apply the same judgment used for ordinary scalar types. This is more likely to expose two kinds of old logic: one treats field names as type text, and the other appends array markers again to an already completed result. Record both cases first, rather than directly altering the strings into a form that merely appears to meet expectations.

### Handle custom errors last

Process error parameter lists after complex types. Record the type input and conversion result for each parameter in the original order, with the error name itself excluded from this migration comparison. If ordinary declarations have passed but error parameters show differences, first check whether the error declaration bypasses centralized conversion; do not change the declaration structure of `CustomError` because of this.

## Follow-up after the caller walkthrough

Subsequent walkthroughs focus on both ends: who receives the type object, and who consumes the signature string. After an actual review of the existing implementation, the related work was handed over to the current module maintainer, so unverified call relationships are not drawn as a complete chain here. Each call site only needs to answer two questions: is the input still a type object, or is it already formatted text; before the output is passed downstream, are parentheses, array markers, or field fragments added again.

If a caller only passes along the result of centralized conversion, it does not need a separate set of compatibility rules. If it retains local assembly logic, first preserve that logic's raw output, then compare it with the centralized conversion result. Do not immediately delete the local code when ordinary types match, and inspect the original paths for aliases, arrays, structures with bounded nesting, and error parameters at least once each. Where there is no evidence of actual calls, leave only items to verify, and do not draw conclusions about calls from path locations.

## Migration batches and stopping points

The first batch only connects ordinary elementary type cases, stopping at the input object and conversion entry point if results are unexpected. The second batch adds aliases, and if differences occur only between the declaration name and the underlying type, revisit the type category without changing the caller's display logic. The third batch adds arrays and struct fields, first inspecting arrays, fields, and nesting levels separately; stop at the conversion point if recursion cannot terminate. Only the fourth batch adds custom error parameters, and if differences unique to the error path are found, revisit only its parameter retrieval and entry-point wiring.

Preserve the old strings for every batch, and do not let the next batch overwrite the previous batch's original values. This distinguishes "the centralized entry point changed the result" from "the call site is still performing a second round of assembly". If a single change replaces type classification, declaration structure, and caller formatting at the same time, only the final text will be visible when it fails, and the local path cannot be restored.

SLT-214 can serve as entry points for returning to the items under inspection. The action left on the card is to run the source code identified in the report once on the current version and circle the specific syntactic units that have changed. The actual review must still use the input types, old results, and new results preserved here as its basis; the card does not replace sample records or prove that all type categories have been checked.

## Restore the old path

The restoration scope includes only the centralized conversion entry point and its caller wiring. If a batch of samples shows unexplained differences, first return that batch's callers to their pre-change string sources while preserving the type inputs and the results on both sides. Do not modify `Context`, replace the declaration structure of `CustomError`, or directly change type aliases into display names just to make the samples pass.

After restoration, review ordinary types, aliases, arrays or struct fields, and error parameters in that order. If ordinary types also change, first check whether the object passed into conversion is no longer the object used in the old path; if only error parameters change, first check whether the error declaration was left disconnected from the centralized entry point. If complex samples change while ordinary samples remain unchanged, retain the complex samples as the failure boundary rather than reverting the entire declaration file.

Another recommendation from the old draft is still retained here: each call site should fill in array markers independently, with variable declarations and error declarations maintaining separate string assembly logic. This passage is no longer an implementation step, but it can be used to locate remaining local concatenation. The post-migration checks focus on ensuring that arrays, aliases, and nested fields of the same type do not once again produce different formats merely because the callers differ.

On completion, it should be possible to trace samples back to explicit input types, conversion points, and caller consumption points; type categories without actual samples remain in the pending-verification column.

# Caller Migration Index for Current and Old Entry Points

What the plugin example project has retained is not a record of directory renames. It collects real call samples involving example and plugin: which callers still come through the old entry point, which can already continue from the replacement location, and whether the issues encountered during the switch concern the integration boundary or the index itself. The entry point file is still at `docs/adj-plugin-example/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Attachments are maintained by the project team; this document records the relationships that must be preserved during migration.

The situation most likely to cause a misjudgment is when the directory already contains a "current entry point," but callers are still working from the old location. Names in the index can only help locate items; they cannot replace confirmation from adopters. Conversely, one call sample reaching the replacement location does not mean that all sources with the same name have migrated. The old entry point, the current entry point, and the caller must be recorded separately.

```text
Old entry point ──retain──> Existing callers
  │                  │
  │                  └──Real call samples
  │
  └──trial integration──> Current entry point / Replacement location ──> Confirmed adopters
                         │
                         └──Return to the old entry point if results differ or calls cannot continue
```

## Start by Recording These Details Separately in the Index

A migration record must answer at least four questions: where the original entry point is; where its intended replacement is; which plugin-example-client-integration caller is using it; and what kind of example or plugin sample that caller is using. The first two describe locations, while the last two describe actual adoption. Do not treat "current entry point" as a name that can be reused arbitrarily; even if two records have the same name, keep them as two rows whenever their sources or adopters differ.

Index entries can be completed in the following order:

| Record section | Information to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry point | The location that callers can still access, and why it is being retained |
| Replacement location | The replacement location that the current entry point actually points to, not a directory alias |
| Caller | Known plugin-example-client-integration adopters |
| Sample | The example, plugin, or combined sample that triggered this migration |
| Trial results | The results observed by the caller after switching, or confirmation that has not yet been received |
| Rollback record | The reason for returning to the old entry point, and whether the old path has been restored |

"Confirmation not yet received" can be written directly in the results field. Do not cover up this field with a green status or a new directory entry. Historical lookups also depend on old records; if only the replacement location is retained, it will be difficult later to distinguish whether an entry point was migrated, a caller was not migrated, or two sources with the same name were incorrectly merged into one.

## Start Each Migration with the Original Sample

First choose a caller that is already in use, rather than creating a new example that looks cleaner. Note where it originally entered, what sample it used, and what could be observed on the first call. What is being preserved here is the actual call scenario, not a tidied-up presentation of the results; if inputs were changed during the trial, the index must also show when those changes occurred.

Next, connect this caller to the replacement location. Do not immediately delete the old entry point or rewrite the old row in the index as a new row. Keeping them side by side for a short time is useful: it lets people confirm whether the caller actually switched or only the directory text changed. The current entry point is available for trial integration, but whether it becomes the official location depends on whether the actual caller can continue working.

When confirming, check only this call sample itself. The migration record must state clearly whether it has left the old entry point or is still completing calls there. Confirmation for one sample cannot establish a conclusion for neighboring samples; different combinations of example and plugin may also have different compatibility boundaries. The index should preserve these differences rather than compressing them into the two overall statuses "migrated" and "not migrated."

If the caller has not yet confirmed, continue listing the old entry point as valid. It may be retained temporarily, or it may be waiting for the adopter to provide results; in either case, the replacement location cannot be used as grounds to claim that the old entry point has been decommissioned.

## Batch Planning

Dividing migration batches by caller is safer than replacing paths all at once. Each batch moves only one identified adopter and retains the sample corresponding to that switch in the index. This way, before work on the second caller has begun, rolling back the first batch will not take subsequent batches back to the old path as well.

Maintain the following continuity across batches:

1. The old entry point field continues to point to the original location until that caller confirms that the replacement location is usable.
2. The current entry point field contains only the replacement location actually used in this batch, without borrowing records with similar names.
3. The caller field contains only adopters that have been observed; do not infer unknown users from path names.
4. The sample field retains the original example, plugin combination so that differences before and after the switch can be reviewed later.
5. The results field first records what has been observed, then whether to proceed; if there are no results, leave it pending confirmation.

Separating things this way also avoids a common problem: when the timing of index updates and caller integration is reversed, what looks like a completed migration is actually just a replacement location that was registered first. When encountering such a record, do not rewrite old rows just to make the sequence tidy. Record entry point registration and adopter integration separately so that the source of the difference can be identified later.

## How to Retain the Old Entry Point

The old entry point is useful even when nothing has gone wrong. Callers that have not yet migrated need it to keep working; callers that have already migrated may also need it to compare against the original sample. Old records in the index should retain the original location, known adopters, and traces of the most recent migration attempt. Do not rename the old entry point to "history" and then remove the adopters, because that would turn the migration scope into a directory state that cannot be verified.

All of the following conditions must be met before maintenance of the old path can stop: identified adopters have continued using the replacement location; the index still allows the old record to be traced back from the replacement location; and there are no pending rollback records. Merely seeing that the current entry point exists, or that one example runs successfully from the new location, is not enough.

Early records treated "the appearance of the current entry point" as a sign that migration was nearly complete. This statement no longer applies. It did not distinguish between the replacement location being ready and callers having adopted it, nor did it preserve the differences between sources with the same name. This assessment is retained to help explain why the old index appeared to be further ahead than the actual migration; subsequent records are to be based on adopters and samples.

## Handling Cases Where Migration Does Not Proceed

If, after trial integration, the caller's results differ from the original sample, or the replacement location cannot continue handling that call, restore the old entry point first. The focus of restoration is to give the original caller a usable location again, not to erase this attempt from the index. The index should retain: which caller was switched, what kind of sample was used, what the replacement location was, and why the caller returned to the old entry point. This prevents the next person taking over from treating the same trial as though it had never happened.

After a rollback, do not also replace other callers' records. One caller returning to the old entry point means that this migration cannot yet proceed; it does not automatically prove that other confirmed adopters must also roll back. Conversely, if the original caller still cannot be found after the old entry point is restored, leave the item unconfirmed rather than recording the restoration as successful.

A rollback can be documented with the following short record:

```text
Caller: Identified plugin-example-client-integration adopter
Original sample: Corresponding example / plugin combination
Trial integration location: Replacement location for the current entry point
Action: Restore the old entry point
Items to retain: Old entry point record, trial integration traces, results pending confirmation
```

This is not a list of commands to execute. The specific entry point is determined by the location in the index; the requirement here is that the original call relationships and the outcome of this trial remain clear after restoration.

## Stopping Points During Index Maintenance

When there is only a name and no adopter, do not classify the entry as migrated yet. A name can be used for lookup, but it does not indicate who is using it.

When there is only a caller and neither the old entry point nor the replacement location can be found, retain the fact that the caller exists and mark the location field as pending completion. Do not guess the source based on similar directories.

When both the old and current entry points have records but the samples differ, the two results cannot be compared directly. First confirm whether they belong to the same caller and the same type of example, plugin usage; if this cannot be confirmed, retain them separately.

After a rollback, the old entry point should once again become that caller's working path. The replacement location may remain in the index, but it must carry a record that this trial integration did not proceed, so that it is not later misread as having been adopted.

When only the replacement location remains in the index, with no confirmation from any caller, migration stops here. Continue after adding the adopter or the original sample; do not substitute directory cleanup for integration feedback.

## Reading Order for Handoffs

First, use `docs/adj-plugin-example/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md` to find the source of the entry with the same name, then check whether it lists an actual adopter. Next, review that caller's corresponding example, plugin samples and most recent trial integration record. If the entry shows traces of a rollback, first confirm whether the old entry point is still usable by this caller; do not move it to the replacement location again until this is confirmed.

This index covers only joint integration testing with callers of plugin example. It retains its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, as well as old notes that cannot be traced back. Entries that cannot be confirmed do not need to be deleted for the sake of tidiness; they at least show that the old entry point was once treated as a migration target, but the available materials still cannot establish who has adopted the replacement location.

# Release Automation: Index of Existing Legacy Entry Points

Record entry point changes for LICENSE · Release Automation individually by legacy entry point. You cannot infer the build queues created by `.github/workflows`, the artifact versions those queues produce, or the artifact rollback windows just because the current entry point appears in the directory. A legacy entry point may still be used by callers, or it may have only untraceable notes left behind; record these two cases separately.

Each index row corresponds to one legacy entry point; do not merge similarly named bypass paths. Keep at least the legacy entry point, replacement location, confirmed callers, associated build queue, artifact versions, and rollback window in each row. The existence of a replacement location only means the migration has a destination, not that callers have switched. If callers are still unconfirmed, leave the status as migration in progress; if a note cannot be traced back, retain its original wording and mark it as outdated. Do not use the display text to fill in its source.

## Record the Switch

1. Start from the legacy entry point and find callers that still use it. Directory searches can only provide leads; determine whether migration is complete based on actual callers. Even if nobody is using it, record the search scope; do not turn "not found" into "not in use".
2. Record a replacement location for each caller and confirm that it enters the build queue for license-release-automation, not merely that the documentation path has changed. For adjacent current revisions, compare only the first path difference; do not merge records just because the two paths are similar.
3. Record the artifact versions associated with this switch under the corresponding batch, along with the rollback window. Until the window closes, the legacy entry point remains an available recovery point; even after it closes, do not remove the legacy path or the last confirmation.
4. After the switch, check whether the build queue is still reading values from the legacy entry point. If any callers remain on the legacy entry point, keep that batch marked as migration in progress; if the new entry point is visible but there is no evidence from callers, do not mark it complete.

If the work needs to be split into batches, attach each batch to the original entry point record and list its callers and artifact versions separately. Keep the independent schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria with this release automation record; do not collapse multiple batches into one final result. If the exit actions have not yet been clearly documented, the entry should explicitly show that a rollback command or stop condition is missing, rather than assume that further switching is allowed.

## Restore the Legacy Entry Point

If the replacement location has a localized problem, first stop migrating any more affected callers to it, and retain the current entry point and the recorded artifact versions. Recovery actions apply only to the corresponding caller and batch: return the caller to the legacy entry point in the index, confirm that it re-enters the original build queue, and check within the rollback window that the required artifacts are still usable. If there is not enough information to confirm the artifact status, record it only as unconfirmed; do not describe the recovery as successful.

A local recovery does not mean the legacy entry point as a whole is re-enabled. Attach recovery records to the specific caller, build batch, and artifact version. When migration resumes, recheck that caller's replacement location rather than reusing the old conclusion for the entire row. After the legacy entry point is retired, continue to retain the legacy entry point, replacement location, last confirmed callers, artifact versions, and rollback window in the index; untraceable notes remain marked as outdated.

# Historical False-Positive Review FAQ

The first answer on this page was once used as the basis for retracting a candidate path, but it was later found to conflate "finding the mapping entry point" with "ruling out the cause of a false positive." The old wording remains because someone actually stopped investigating on that basis during a postmortem; do not close candidate paths based on that old answer again.

**source-mapping What can the entry point establish?**
It only shows that a given candidate path can continue through the existing source-mapping entry point to trace the relevant mapping; it does not mean that the path has been disproved. If adjacent failing samples still land in the same place, the entry point is instead the starting point for continued comparison. The early wording, "the false positive is probably not here," no longer applies: it was a quick judgment based on the presence of the entry point and did not include regression results.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing a candidate path?**
The old practice was for the person who proposed the path to write the reason for withdrawing it next to the original postmortem record, while others only added counterexamples. This division still preserves the source of the judgment, but it does not solve who writes it down after the proposer leaves. Do not cross out a candidate just because someone says "it doesn't look like it" in a discussion; at minimum, leave the failing samples that were compared. If the proposer cannot be reached, this page names no replacement, and the original record remains unretracted.

**Under what conditions can it be closed?**
The team's standard at the time was that the compatibility card could enter the closed state only if the adjacent failing samples, existing package imports, and non-author regressions all passed. Here, "all pass" means conjunctive conditions, not a choice of one. The source-mapping entry point can help locate the comparison targets, but it does not substitute for any of the three.

Python imports and CLI exit-code records are a separate question. Someone wanted to include them in the closure materials, but the existing postmortem contains no record sufficient to determine whether they are necessary, so their absence cannot be recorded directly as a failure, nor can they be added as established gates. For follow-up on the single-variable rerun from that time, the relevant notes are recorded in DOC-50; this page retains only these three questions and the old standard used at the time.

During a postmortem, record entry-point identification, candidate withdrawal, and card closure separately. With only entry-point information, the record stops at "the candidate path still needs comparison"; even with failing samples, it can only indicate that a review is needed, and cannot replace the withdrawal rationale left by the proposer. If the original record has no person assigned to withdraw it, the issue is not automatically transferred to the person who found the counterexample; the record remains unretracted.

One final point that is easy to misread: withdrawing a candidate path does not mean that the cause of the false positive has been identified; closing the compatibility card does not mean that every local troubleshooting action has complete output recorded. The two often appeared together in the old postmortems, which caused the conflation above.

The purpose of this record is not to explain the entire interface, but to make clear to the next person on call that the comparison did not change multiple conditions at once.

The first draft treated "the first run after rollback ran to completion" as a rough indication that the interface had recovered. Reviewing the raw logs showed that this wording was too strong: the first run only showed that the entry point used at the time did not immediately produce the old behavior; it could not substitute for confirming the call relationships. - Repository state for cli-packaging;
- Call entry point for the static analysis interface;
- Raw logs from the first run after rollback.
