# Upstream Compatibility Window Decision Record

Cliff Security Lab began this wrap-up discussion not with a completed compatibility matrix, but with a narrower question: in response to upstream changes, whether to adjust the window immediately or retain the current analysis-core entry point and first fix in place the portions already checked. Both approaches can be described as "maintaining compatibility", but their evidence requirements are not the same.

The earliest record focused on the public calls in the frozen repository and a point of divergence in a failure that was reproducible at the time. The purpose was not to elevate a single failure into the entire conclusion, but to prevent the review from inferring responsibility from names. If parsing, analysis, and output were first lumped together into a single "compatibility issue", even a later successful run would not make it possible to explain in retrospect which entry point or processing stage had changed, or whether only the presentation of the results was different.

This decision retains the exact wording from the review materials: "Preserve the original failure, do not overwrite the first divergence with a later successful run". Here, "preserve" has a very specific meaning. The first failure should continue to point to the public call and divergence location at that time; it explains why the scope needs to be frozen. If a later successful run occurs, it can only serve as another observation: it may prompt a recheck, or reveal that the earlier attribution was too broad, but it cannot erase the first divergence from the materials.

## The Two Options Presented at the Time

There was no third, compromise formulation in the discussion. The only two options on the table were retaining the entry point and adjusting the window; the difference was the scope of judgment to be taken on in this round.

| Approach | Action recorded in this round | Supporting materials available at the time | Remaining cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current analysis-core entry point | Continue checking along the public calls in the frozen repository and fix the scope covered by existing evidence | Public calls, a reproducible failure, and its first divergence | Areas outside the entry point receive no compatibility conclusion from this freeze |
| Adjust the upstream compatibility window | Include more upstream boundaries in this round's assessment and change the scope of the existing window | Call evidence for the added boundaries and corresponding failure rechecks are required | If the materials are insufficient, unresolved responsibilities will be written into commitments prematurely |

The first option is not "ignoring upstream", nor does it leave the failure to be examined later. It limits this round's action to retaining the entry point that has actually been examined, and acknowledges that gaps remain outside the window. The second option is not inherently wrong either; if there are clear public calls, reproduced failures, and assessments across layers for the added boundaries, it could become a candidate decision for the next review. The issue is that this round's materials do not provide these additions, and a broader label cannot replace them.

Therefore, the decision in this round is to retain the current analysis-core entry point and freeze the compatibility scope covered by existing evidence. Here, "freeze" only means not expanding further into unchecked upstream boundaries during this wrap-up; it does not mean that all upstream cases have been confirmed, much less that cases outside the window must fail. Areas outside the window have only one status in this record: not yet confirmed in this round's materials.

## Why the Three Layers Must Be Separated

A recurring risk in the review was attributing an observed behavior directly to the "compatibility layer". That term is too broad to guide whether the entry point should change. The parsing layer handles how input enters the compatibility assessment; the analysis layer handles how it is analyzed once it enters; the output layer handles how results are recorded. The three can appear next to one another in the same run, but they are not the same point of responsibility.

If a failure occurs before the input is interpreted, a subsequent change in output does not automatically show that the parsing layer has recovered; if the analysis has already produced a different result, normal-looking output text alone cannot prove that the analysis layer has fulfilled its responsibility. Conversely, a difference at the output layer does not directly imply that the entry point for analysis-core needs to change. The review uses a layered description so that any window adjustment must answer a specific question: which layer the added boundary actually changes, rather than making a broad judgment based only on a single end-to-end run.

This also explains why a "later successful run" cannot replace the first failure. A successful run records a result that appeared later; the first failure records the location of the initial divergence. Together, they can trigger a recheck, but none of the materials permit combining them into "the earlier failure has been disproven" or "the entire window has passed". In the decision text, the two observations serve different roles and cannot overwrite each other.

## Why Adjusting the Window Was Not Adopted

Adjusting the window means including additional upstream boundaries in this round's conclusion. Doing so requires, at a minimum, identifying the public call through which each added boundary enters and assigning the failure location to the parsing, analysis, or output layer. The existing materials support comparing the two approaches and retaining the current entry point, but they do not confirm these additional relationships one by one.

If the window were expanded anyway, the most likely outcome would not be an obvious error, but wording finalized before the judgment is complete. Readers would see that the scope had widened, but would not see the corresponding public calls or know whether the reproducible failure actually fell within the added boundaries. Writing it this way would disguise "not yet checked" as "already included within compatibility responsibility", causing the next round's recheck to lose its original starting point.

Another approach discussed was to treat a later successful run as sufficient grounds for adjusting the scope. This approach was not adopted. A success can suggest that the first failure was not a consistent result, or that some condition was different later; but it does not itself define the entry-point boundaries. It cannot replace checking the public calls, nor can it prove that the parsing, analysis, and output layers underwent the same kind of check. Elevating a success record into grounds for the window would only make the decision depend on a result that does not identify where responsibility lies.

Another seemingly simpler wording option was to leave the window text unchanged while implying in a comment that "a broader range of upstream cases is actually already covered". This was not included in the decision either. It would create two sets of claims about the entry point, the window, and the actual scope of assessment. If the scope has in fact changed, the adjustment option should be explicitly adopted at the next review; if the scope has not yet changed, the current entry point should be retained, and the items awaiting confirmation should remain in the reservations.

## Lookup Location Recorded During the Recheck

The subsequent recheck followed the public calls and call names in the frozen repository back to `slither/core/source_mapping/source_mapping.py`. This path is where the lookup actually landed, making it easier for reviewers to return to the materials from that time; it is not a permanent declaration of ownership over the entire compatibility chain. The filename and path themselves cannot substitute for call relationships, nor should they be expanded into an end-to-end path that does not appear in the record.

The recheck maintained the original order: first examine the relationship between the public calls and the first failure, then discuss responsibility across layers, and finally determine whether the window needs to change. This order avoided jumping directly from a file location to a conclusion about scope. The path can show where the investigation continued at that time, but cannot establish on its own that there are grounds for adjusting the window.

What the recheck actually added was constraints on the original judgment, not a complete reversal. The decision to retain the current entry point remains valid because its premise has always been "the scope covered by existing evidence"; the recheck did not provide enough material to include the added boundaries in the decision. The original failure also remains preserved as the first divergence and has not been replaced by the behavior of later runs.

## Boundaries of the Decision's Applicability

This decision only addresses whether the upstream compatibility window changes during this round's wrap-up. It does not replace item-by-item judgments about each parsing, analysis, or output behavior, nor does it generalize a localized observation at one layer into a comprehensive upstream commitment. Anyone who needs to expand the scope should first bring back new public calls and failure materials that can be rechecked, then explain which of the three layers' responsibilities those materials relate to.

This boundary also keeps the reservations readable. Areas outside the window are not known failures, not known successes, and not a permanently excluded region; they simply have no conclusion in this round's evidence. Describing them as unknown is closer to the state of the review at the time than prematurely offering an optimistic or pessimistic judgment.

If adjusting the window is discussed again in the future, the discussion should start with the added entry points, not with "there was a successful run last time". It will then be necessary to confirm whether the same failure divergence can still be rechecked and determine whether the relevant changes belong to parsing, analysis, or output. Only when these relationships can be clearly explained can adjusting the window avoid becoming a label that bundles several different issues together.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Public calls in the frozen repository] --> B[Preserve the first reproducible failure]
    B --> C{Distinguish parsing, analysis, and output}
    C --> D[Freeze the scope covered by existing evidence]
    C --> E[Window adjustment not adopted for now]
```

The diagram preserves the order of judgments in this round. It does not label areas outside the window as failures, nor does it place a later successful run before the first divergence. The grounds for freezing the scope come from the entry points and failures already examined; the adjustment proposal remains among the reservations because materials on the added boundaries are missing.

For the handover covering the solc version pool's rotation change, see DOC-52 separately. The two records are adjacent, but address different subjects: DOC-51 records the options, decision, and reservations for this round's compatibility window; DOC-52 records the handover details for the version pool switch. The version pool record is not used here to fill in the call or failure evidence required for a window adjustment.

The current conclusion does not permanently rule out adjusting the window. It only confirms that, given the available materials, retaining the current analysis-core entry point is more accurate than expanding the scope. Whether the window changes should be left to a subsequent review that can supply the additional public calls, failure divergences, and assessments of responsibility across layers.

# solc version pool rotation handoff guide

The handoff still starts at the old entry point, `slither/core/source_mapping/source_mapping.py`. Here, "old" refers to the entry point before lookup and switchover; it does not mean the file can already be deleted. No separate, confirmed filename has been established for the new path either; this page calls it the candidate path to avoid presenting a lookup location as a permanent home.

```text
Old entry point: source_mapping.py / known calls
        └─ Inventory the callers first
              └─ Select one consumer that can revert on its own for a trial
                    └─ Record the first difference and confirm the maintainer
                          ├─ Acceptable: stay on the candidate path
                          └─ Unacceptable: restore the old entry point
```

## Handoff sequence

1. First, inventory the known consumers and old entry points for source-mapping. Base the caller list on actual calls; do not substitute module names for callers. Mark anything not yet known as unknown, and do not treat file locations found in a search as call relationships.
2. Choose one consumer from the list that can revert on its own. Have it try the candidate path first; no other consumers should switch at the same time. This keeps the first difference tied to that caller and provides a clear stopping point if something goes wrong.
3. During the trial, record the solc version, Python version, and first visible difference side by side. A difference may be a change in results, a change in error location, or no output; record only what was actually observed, not expected results.
4. Have that consumer perform the revert, and record whether it completed. A revert is not just saying "we can roll back"; you must be able to identify the action that restores the old entry point and the observations after restoration.
5. After the trial, find a module maintainer who can continue the verification. The maintainer needs to be able to follow up on all three—the candidate path, versions, and differences—not just passively receive a switchover notification.

Complete the handoff record in the following order; do not fill in conclusions first:

| Item | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry point | `slither/core/source_mapping/source_mapping.py` |
| Candidate path | Version pool rotation switchover; exact location to be confirmed |
| Known callers | TODO: fill in the list based on actual calls |
| Trial consumer | TODO: select a consumer that can revert on its own |
| solc / Python | TODO: enter the actual versions in the trial environment |
| First difference | TODO: enter the first visible change |
| Maintainer | TODO: confirm a module maintainer who can continue handling this |
| Revert result | TODO: enter the result after restoring the old entry point |

## Batches and stopping points

Do not treat all consumers as a single batch in this handoff. The first batch includes only the selected trial consumer; only after it has validated the candidate path and recorded the revert result will there be a basis for deciding whether to proceed. The boundaries of later batches have not yet been settled; "full switchover" is no substitute for a list.

If the trial consumer cannot revert on its own, or the revert action has no recorded result, the handoff remains mid-migration. Without the solc or Python version, differences cannot be attributed to the version pool either; without the first difference, it is impossible to tell whether the candidate path was actually used. Without a maintainer, the page only retains the handoff record and does not declare the switchover complete.

To restore the old path, first stop the trial on the candidate path, then restore the old entry point and observe the same caller again. Do not turn the restoration action into an account of a successful rollback; this record only requires the actions, environment, and results. Wherever specific results have not been added, leave TODO in place.

## Reminders from the old draft

The early records only knew to "follow source-mapping to find the entry point," without a complete caller list, versions, or differences. Retain that assessment, but no longer treat a path found by lookup as a conclusion about ownership. DOC-01 can provide reference material on adjacent call relationships; it cannot replace this page's trial and revert records.

The handoff must retain actual calls, the solc or Python version, the first visible difference, and a module maintainer who can continue the verification. If either the caller inventory or the revert action is missing, the page remains mid-migration.
